Documents required: Passport plus a second ID or proof of foreign address; SIN not required for a basic account; banks may ask for immigration documents.
Minimum deposit & fees: Not published for non-residents; fees vary by package and bank.
Banks accepting non-residents: RBC, TD, Scotiabank, BMO, CIBC (branch opening; newcomer programs target people relocating).
Restrictions: Bank Act/FCAC gives anyone with acceptable ID the right to a basic account, but branches usually require an in-person visit; FATCA/CRS reporting applies.
Alternatives (fintech / regional): Wise CAD account details; Scotiabank/RBC newcomer pre-arrival applications for visa holders.
Cost note: No non-resident tariff published by RBC/TD/Scotiabank/BMO/CIBC (fees vary by package and branches only open for people relocating), and the fee schedule could not be verified this pass, so all figures are null.

Documents required: Passport plus secondary ID, foreign address proof, and usually an SSN or ITIN; some branches accept passport-only for non-resident aliens with a W-8BEN.
Minimum deposit & fees: Varies by bank; typical checking accounts have no or low opening deposit and monthly fees of about USD 5-15 unless waived.
Banks accepting non-residents: Bank of America, Chase, Citibank, PNC, Wells Fargo (branch visit, ITIN accepted by several).
Restrictions: Most major banks require an in-person US branch visit; heavy KYC and de-risking of non-residents; W-8BEN and FATCA/CRS reporting apply.
Alternatives (fintech / regional): Wise USD account details, Revolut, Zolve, Payoneer; Mercury/Relay only for US LLC business accounts.
Cost note: Chase Total Checking: no opening fee or minimum opening deposit, USD 15 monthly service fee (raised from USD 12 in Aug 2025) waivable with USD 500 direct deposits or a USD 1,500 daily balance; already in USD.

Documents required: Passport plus Cuban residence status or Central Bank authorisation; in practice local residency documents are needed.
Minimum deposit & fees: not published
Banks accepting non-residents: Banco Metropolitano, Banco Popular de Ahorro and Banco de Credito y Comercio (USD accounts mainly for Cubans abroad, not foreign non-residents).
Restrictions: US embargo and OFAC sanctions, de-risking by foreign correspondents, dual-currency and FX shortages; Resolution 73/2020 USD accounts target Cuban nationals abroad.
Alternatives (fintech / regional): Visitors rely on cash (EUR/CAD) and prepaid tourist cards; remittance channels via authorised agents; Australian-issued non-US cards may work at some ATMs.
Cost note: Non-residents cannot open personal accounts (Cuban banks' USD accounts target Cubans abroad), so no applicable costs.

Documents required: Passport (notarised copy if by post), proof of foreign address, existing-bank reference letter, foreign TIN or Jamaican TRN, source of funds.
Minimum deposit & fees: Scotiabank Jamaica lists minimum opening balances of about 100 for foreign-currency savings up to JMD 5,000-10,000 for chequing/savings; monthly fees vary by account.
Banks accepting non-residents: National Commercial Bank (NCB), Scotiabank Jamaica.
Restrictions: NCB requires non-residents to open in person at a branch; enhanced KYC and FATCA/CRS reporting apply; USD accounts available.
Alternatives (fintech / regional): Wise or Revolut for JMD transfers; remittance services; no local fintech accounts for non-residents.
Cost note: Scotiabank Jamaica JMD chequing/savings minimum opening balance JMD 5,000-10,000 (lower bound used, about USD 31 at JMD 160/USD; USD foreign-currency savings minimum is USD 100); a current opening fee and monthly fee for these accounts were not found in a published tariff (older 2016 brochure showed JMD 0-600/month), so those are null.

Documents required: Passport, second ID, proof of foreign address, bank/professional reference letters, proof of income and source-of-wealth documentation, stated reason for banking in the Bahamas.
Minimum deposit & fees: Varies by bank; guides cite roughly USD 10,000-250,000 for non-resident/offshore accounts, higher for private banking; fees not published.
Banks accepting non-residents: Mainly international/private banks rather than retail banks; specific accepting banks not confirmed from official pages.
Restrictions: Exchange controls administered by the Central Bank of The Bahamas; only authorised dealers may offer foreign-currency accounts; strong CRS/FATCA and AML scrutiny, many retail banks serve residents only.
Alternatives (fintech / regional): Wise or Revolut from Australia for multi-currency needs; offshore private banks elsewhere.
Cost note: Guides cite USD 10,000-250,000 minimum for non-resident/offshore accounts at international/private banks (low end used, already USD); opening and monthly fees are not published.

Documents required: Passport, proof of foreign address, tax identification number, bank reference letter or statements, source-of-funds/income evidence; some banks ask for local ties.
Minimum deposit & fees: Consultancy sources cite opening deposits from about USD 10,000 depending on account type; bank fees not published for non-residents.
Banks accepting non-residents: CIBC Caribbean (FirstCaribbean), RBC Royal Bank, Republic Bank, First Citizens, Sagicor Bank; acceptance of non-residents varies by bank and profile.
Restrictions: Heavy KYC/CRS and FATCA reporting; many banks require economic ties to Barbados; Barbados exchange controls apply to BBD accounts, foreign-currency accounts need approval.
Alternatives (fintech / regional): Wise or Revolut for multi-currency needs; offshore/international banks in Barbados for higher-net-worth clients.
Cost note: Consultancy sources cite opening deposits from about USD 10,000 (already USD) depending on bank and account type; no Barbadian bank publishes a non-resident opening or monthly fee, so those are null.

Documents required: Two forms of ID (one must be a passport), proof of foreign address, proof of income and a bank reference; branch visit required.
Minimum deposit & fees: Opening deposit required but amount not published for non-residents.
Banks accepting non-residents: First Citizens Bank (publishes non-resident requirements); Republic Bank (non-resident category, branch only).
Restrictions: Online onboarding (RepublicOnboard) is for nationals; USD/foreign-currency availability is constrained by chronic FX shortages; strict AML/KYC and CRS/FATCA reporting.
Alternatives (fintech / regional): Wise or Revolut for holding/paying in USD; TT dollar local details not offered by major fintechs.
Cost note: First Citizens and Republic Bank require an opening deposit for non-residents but publish no amount, opening fee or monthly fee, so all three are null as unpublished.

Documents required: Passport, proof of foreign address (utility bill), bank reference letter, source-of-funds declaration, TIN if available.
Minimum deposit & fees: Guides cite from about XCD 300 at local banks up to around USD 5,000 at international-oriented banks; fees not published.
Banks accepting non-residents: Global Bank of Commerce, ACB Caribbean, Republic Bank (Antigua) cited by guides; Canadian banks reported exiting.
Restrictions: Strict KYC/AML and CRS reporting to home tax authority; correspondent de-risking means scrutiny of non-resident clients; US persons face FATCA.
Alternatives (fintech / regional): Wise or Revolut held abroad; offshore/international banks licensed by the FSRC.
Cost note: Cheapest cited option is a local bank opening deposit of about XCD 300 (USD 1 = XCD 2.70, fixed peg), while opening and monthly fees are not published (web search budget exhausted in pass 2, so figures come from the existing min_deposit_fees text and were not re-verified against a bank tariff).

Documents required: Passport plus second ID, proof of foreign address, bank reference letter, proof of income and source-of-funds documentation; banks may ask for a Grenada visa or residence.
Minimum deposit & fees: Not published by banks; guides cite opening deposits from zero to about USD 10,000.
Banks accepting non-residents: Republic Bank (Grenada), ACB Grenada, CIBC FirstCaribbean, Grenada Co-operative Bank (case-by-case for non-residents).
Restrictions: Banks generally decline short-stay tourists; enhanced KYC, FATCA/CRS reporting and Caribbean correspondent-bank de-risking limit non-resident onboarding.
Alternatives (fintech / regional): Wise or Revolut for multi-currency needs; Grenada citizenship-by-investment holders get easier access.
Cost note: Republic Bank, ACB and CIBC FirstCaribbean publish no non-resident tariff; guides cite opening deposits from zero to about USD 10,000 (XCD 2.70/USD), so all figures are unpublished.

Documents required: Passport, proof of foreign address, bank reference letter, 6 months of bank statements and source-of-funds evidence; certified/notarised copies if remote.
Minimum deposit & fees: Reported XCD 100-700 for basic local accounts and USD 10,000-50,000 for international/non-resident accounts (unverified).
Banks accepting non-residents: Republic Bank, Bank of Nevis, St Kitts-Nevis-Anguilla National Bank, CIBC FirstCaribbean.
Restrictions: Enhanced due diligence and higher balances for non-residents; CIBC online opening limited to residents.
Alternatives (fintech / regional): Wise USD details; regional Caribbean or US accounts.
Cost note: Minimum deposit is the low end of the reported (unverified) USD 10,000-50,000 for international/non-resident accounts at local banks; opening and monthly fees are not published.

Documents required: Passport (notarised copies if not original), proof of foreign address, bank reference letter from a bank of 3+ years' relationship, source of funds, CRS/FATCA self-certification.
Minimum deposit & fees: Not published officially; guides cite roughly USD 5,000 for non-residents, older reports far lower.
Banks accepting non-residents: Bank of Saint Lucia (dedicated non-national/non-resident customer type), 1st National Bank St Lucia, Republic Bank (EC).
Restrictions: Strict correspondent-banking KYC; Hermes Bank in liquidation since 2025; XCD pegged to USD.
Alternatives (fintech / regional): Wise, Revolut (no local EC dollar details); citizenship-by-investment holders get easier access.
Cost note: Minimum deposit is the roughly USD 5,000 non-resident figure cited by third-party guides (not an official Bank of Saint Lucia tariff); opening and monthly fees are not published.

Documents required: Passport (notarised copy), proof of foreign address, bank reference letter, source-of-funds evidence, TIN for CRS.
Minimum deposit & fees: Not published for personal accounts; BOSVG lists a nominal opening deposit (about XCD 10) on its account checklist.
Banks accepting non-residents: Bank of St. Vincent and the Grenadines (accepts notarised forms by email/fax); Republic Bank (EC) via RepublicOnboard is aimed at nationals abroad.
Restrictions: Enhanced due diligence for non-residents, CRS reporting, correspondent-bank de-risking in the Eastern Caribbean; XCD pegged to USD.
Alternatives (fintech / regional): Wise or Revolut for multi-currency needs; offshore-oriented international banks licensed in SVG serve non-residents but are not retail banks.
Cost note: Bank of St. Vincent and the Grenadines checklist cites a nominal opening deposit of about XCD 10 (about USD 3.70 at XCD 2.70/USD); opening and monthly fees for non-resident personal accounts are not published.

Documents required: Passport, second ID, proof of foreign address (utility bill), bank reference, source-of-funds evidence.
Minimum deposit & fees: not published
Banks accepting non-residents: National Bank of Dominica (case-by-case); other onshore banks not confirmed.
Restrictions: Enhanced due diligence for non-residents and CBI-linked clients; EC dollar pegged to USD at 2.70; correspondent-banking de-risking in the Eastern Caribbean limits USD services.
Alternatives (fintech / regional): Wise or Revolut transfers; offshore banks under the Financial Services Unit; regional banks in other ECCU states.
Cost note: National Bank of Dominica handles non-residents case-by-case and publishes no non-resident opening fee, minimum deposit or monthly fee, so all three are null.

Documents required: Passport with valid entry stamp, second ID, proof of foreign address, home-bank reference letter (often in Spanish), proof of income/source of funds, FATCA/CRS forms.
Minimum deposit & fees: Low; guides cite about USD 100-500 opening deposit (Banreservas USD account reported around USD 300); monthly fees not published.
Banks accepting non-residents: Banco Popular Dominicano, Banreservas, BHD, Scotiabank (practice varies by branch).
Restrictions: Usually savings accounts only for non-residents; branch-level discretion and frequent refusals; overstayed tourists cannot open; withdrawal limits and fees vary.
Alternatives (fintech / regional): Wise or Revolut for transfers; local remittance services.
Cost note: Banreservas USD account reported at about USD 300 opening deposit (guides cite USD 100-500, already USD); opening and monthly fees are not published for non-residents.

Documents required: Passport or ID, residence permit (often), proof of address, completed application; diaspora remote openings use notarized signatures by mail.
Minimum deposit & fees: US trade guide cites a minimum deposit of HTG 2,500 for individual accounts; fees not published.
Banks accepting non-residents: Unibank (diaspora account-from-abroad process reported), Sogebank, BNC; non-resident foreigner acceptance case-by-case.
Restrictions: Severe security crisis and gang violence disrupt branches; correspondent-banking de-risking limits USD transfers; strict AML checks.
Alternatives (fintech / regional): Mobile money (MonCash, Natcash) requires local SIM/ID; remittance services such as Western Union or Remitly for sending funds.
Cost note: US trade guide cites a minimum deposit of HTG 2,500 for individual accounts (about USD 19 at roughly HTG 131 = USD 1); opening and monthly fees are not published by Unibank, Sogebank or BNC.

Documents required: Passport, Mexican residence card (temporal/permanente) for most banks, proof of address under 3 months old, tax ID (RFC or foreign TIN); tourists on an FMM generally refused.
Minimum deposit & fees: Not published for non-residents; some banks impose minimum balances and withdrawal limits on non-resident accounts.
Banks accepting non-residents: Some branches of major banks (e.g. BBVA México, Banamex, Banorte) open accounts case-by-case; most require residency.
Restrictions: Almost all banks require residency; non-resident accounts often restricted (card-only, transfer limits); USD accounts limited to border-zone residents; CRS/FATCA reporting.
Alternatives (fintech / regional): Wise (MXN transfers), Revolut; digital banks offering card-only wallets without residency.
Cost note: No bank named publishes a non-resident personal tariff (BBVA Mexico, Banamex and Banorte open non-resident accounts case-by-case with unpublished minimum balances), so all three figures are left null as unpublished.

Documents required: Passport with entry stamp, local proof of address (hotel/lease letter), NIT tax ID from SAT, home bank reference letter, initial deposit.
Minimum deposit & fees: Reports range from about GTQ 500 to USD 1,000+ for USD accounts; not officially published.
Banks accepting non-residents: Banco Industrial and BAM reported as most flexible for foreigners.
Restrictions: Physical presence usually required; branch-level discretion is high; USD accounts subject to extra KYC and source-of-funds checks.
Alternatives (fintech / regional): Wise or Revolut cards for local ATM use; remittance services.
Cost note: Banco Industrial/BAM opening deposit reported from about GTQ 500 (USD 1 = GTQ 7.7), with USD accounts needing USD 1,000+, and opening and monthly fees not published (web search budget exhausted in pass 2, so figures come from the existing min_deposit_fees text and were not re-verified against a bank tariff).

Documents required: Passport, proof of foreign address, bank reference, proof of income and source of wealth, CRS/FATCA self-certification; onboarding by video call and email.
Minimum deposit & fees: Guides cite minimum deposits around USD 1,000-5,000; fees not published.
Banks accepting non-residents: Offshore/international banks such as Belize Bank International and Heritage International Bank accept non-residents; domestic banks vary.
Restrictions: Offshore (international) banks hold foreign-currency accounts only; domestic BZD accounts usually need residency; strict source-of-funds checks and CRS reporting.
Alternatives (fintech / regional): Wise, Revolut for everyday use.
Cost note: Third-party guides cite minimum opening deposits of about USD 1,000-5,000 at international banks such as Belize Bank International (BZD 2.00/USD peg), and 1,000 is the lower bound; opening and monthly fees are not published.

Documents required: Passport, Salvadoran tax number (NIT), description of expected activity; higher-risk clients add income proof or tax returns.
Minimum deposit & fees: Not published; varies by bank.
Banks accepting non-residents: Banco Agrícola, Banco Cuscatlán, Davivienda, Promerica (in-person, case by case).
Restrictions: 2025 guidelines tier foreign clients by risk; banks look for a local tie (NIT, address, representative); USD is the official currency.
Alternatives (fintech / regional): Wise USD account; Chivo/Bitcoin wallets outside banking.
Cost note: Banco Agricola, Cuscatlan, Davivienda and Promerica do not publish non-resident opening requirements or fees (case-by-case in branch), so all figures are null.

Documents required: Passport with valid entry stamp, proof of address, bank reference letters; many banks want a Honduran residency card or RTN tax number.
Minimum deposit & fees: Not published.
Banks accepting non-residents: BAC Credomatic, Banco Ficohsa, Banco Atlantida, Davivienda (case-by-case for non-residents).
Restrictions: Banks historically discouraged from opening accounts for foreigners without residency; approval at branch manager discretion; remote opening mainly for Hondurans abroad.
Alternatives (fintech / regional): Wise, Revolut, remittance services (e.g. Western Union).
Cost note: Honduras: not published by the banks named and no official tariff could be found, so all three figures are left null.

Documents required: Passport with entry stamp, second photo ID, proof of foreign address, bank reference letters, income statement, sometimes two local references.
Minimum deposit & fees: Low minimums reported, e.g. about USD 50-100 or NIO 1,000 for savings; fees not published.
Banks accepting non-residents: BAC Credomatic, Banpro, LAFISE (case-by-case for non-residents, branch visit required).
Restrictions: US and EU sanctions on officials and state entities, 2024 laws widening state access to financial data, heavy KYC; USD accounts common.
Alternatives (fintech / regional): Wise or Revolut abroad; remittance services such as Xoom deliver to local accounts.
Cost note: Reported minimum opening deposits at BAC/Banpro/LAFISE are about USD 50-100 (lower bound used) or NIO 1,000 (about USD 27 at NIO 36.6/USD); opening and monthly fees are not published.

Documents required: Passport with entry stamp, proof of foreign address, source-of-funds documents, sometimes a bank reference; full accounts usually need a DIMEX residence card.
Minimum deposit & fees: Simplified non-resident accounts typically capped around USD 1,200-2,000 in monthly deposits; opening deposit and fees not published.
Banks accepting non-residents: Banco de Costa Rica (BCR) offers limited non-resident accounts; private banks such as BAC Credomatic case-by-case.
Restrictions: Non-resident accounts carry monthly deposit caps and limited products; strict AML/KYC under SUGEF; branch acceptance is inconsistent.
Alternatives (fintech / regional): Wise or Revolut for CRC transfers; keep funds in a home-country account.
Cost note: Banco de Costa Rica simplified non-resident accounts cap monthly deposits at about USD 1,200-2,000, but no opening fee, minimum deposit or monthly fee is published, so all three are null.

Documents required: Passport plus second ID, one or two bank reference letters, professional reference, proof of address, proof of income, source-of-funds statement, CV; remote applications usually need notarised or apostilled copies.
Minimum deposit & fees: Varies widely; guides cite about USD 1,000-10,000, some banks up to USD 250,000 for non-residents; fees not published.
Banks accepting non-residents: Specific accepting banks not confirmed from official pages; acceptance is bank-by-bank and often via a local attorney introduction.
Restrictions: Heavy AML/KYC due diligence and frequent unexplained rejections; FATCA forms for US persons; dollarised economy so USD accounts are standard.
Alternatives (fintech / regional): Wise or Revolut; Panama-based EMIs not established for non-residents.
Cost note: Guides cite USD 1,000-10,000 (some banks up to USD 250,000) minimum for non-residents, low end used and already in USD; opening and monthly fees are not published.

Documents required: Passport plus, at most banks, cedula de extranjeria (requires visa over 3 months), Colombian address and phone, proof of income; branch visit required.
Minimum deposit & fees: Personal accounts reported from about USD 50 initial deposit; non-resident fees not published.
Banks accepting non-residents: Bancolombia and Davivienda generally require cedula; BBVA Colombia reportedly opens some accounts in person with passport only.
Restrictions: SARLAFT AML screening lets banks refuse non-residents; foreign-exchange registration rules (Banco de la Republica) for inbound funds; 4x1000 financial transactions tax.
Alternatives (fintech / regional): Nequi and Daviplata digital wallets accept passports with low limits; Wise or Revolut for international transfers.
Cost note: Personal accounts are reported to open with about USD 50 initial deposit (secondary sources, roughly COP 200,000 at COP 4,000 = USD 1); Bancolombia, Davivienda and BBVA Colombia do not publish non-resident opening or monthly fees.

Documents required: Venezuelan cédula de identidad and RIF tax ID, local proof of address, proof of income and personal/bank references; in-branch processing.
Minimum deposit & fees: Not published.
Banks accepting non-residents: None known for non-residents; Banco de Venezuela, Banco Mercantil and BNC require local cédula/RIF and Venezuelan address.
Restrictions: US OFAC and other sanctions on the government and state banks, severe correspondent-banking de-risking, hyperinflation history and exchange controls; USD access largely via cash or Zelle-type informal channels.
Alternatives (fintech / regional): Foreigners typically use home-country accounts with cash USD, Zinli/Binance P2P or employer-managed accounts; no mainstream fintech local details.
Cost note: Non-residents cannot realistically open a personal account here, so no opening fee, minimum deposit or monthly fee applies or is published.

Documents required: Passport, usually a valid visa or cedula, proof of address, employment certificate or RUC, personal reference from an Ecuadorian citizen.
Minimum deposit & fees: not published
Banks accepting non-residents: Banco Pichincha (passport plus visa reported), BanEcuador (accepts passport), some savings cooperatives.
Restrictions: Most banks require a cedula (residency); economy is dollarised so accounts are in USD; strict AML checks on foreign funds.
Alternatives (fintech / regional): Savings and credit cooperatives; Wise/Revolut for USD; foreign cards at ATMs.
Cost note: Banco Pichincha, BanEcuador and cooperatives publish no non-resident opening fee, minimum deposit or monthly fee (web search budget exhausted in pass 2, so figures come from the existing min_deposit_fees text and were not re-verified against a bank tariff).

Documents required: Passport (at least 6 months validity); most banks want a Carné de Extranjería, Peruvian address proof (rental contract, utility bill) and local phone.
Minimum deposit & fees: Not published for non-residents; basic accounts typically have no minimum deposit.
Banks accepting non-residents: BCP, Interbank, BBVA Peru, Scotiabank Peru (mostly residents; passport-only basic accounts case-by-case).
Restrictions: Most banks require residency in practice; a 2025 SBS rule reportedly allows passport-only basic accounts but with limits; physical presence needed.
Alternatives (fintech / regional): Wise, Revolut; local wallets Yape/Plin need a Peruvian bank account.
Cost note: Basic soles savings accounts at BCP, Interbank and BBVA typically have no minimum deposit (PEN 3.7/USD), but no non-resident fee schedule is published for opening or monthly fees.

Documents required: Passport, foreigner ID card (carnet de extranjero) from temporary residence, NIT, local proof of address.
Minimum deposit & fees: Reported about USD 50-1,000 (often ~USD 100) initial deposit for residents.
Banks accepting non-residents: none known for non-residents (Banco Nacional de Bolivia, Mercantil Santa Cruz, BISA serve residents).
Restrictions: Tourists cannot open accounts; FX shortages and 2026 currency changes; source-of-funds checks on USD deposits above USD 5,000.
Alternatives (fintech / regional): Wise or home-country accounts; local cash.
Cost note: Non-residents cannot open personal accounts here, so all cost fields are null; resident accounts reportedly need about USD 50-1,000 (often ~USD 100) initial deposit.

Documents required: Passport, proof of address (utility bill), proof of income, Guyana TIN certificate, and a banker's reference for foreign nationals.
Minimum deposit & fees: Republic Bank Guyana savings minimums cited from GYD 5,000 to GYD 100,000 depending on product.
Banks accepting non-residents: Republic Bank (Guyana) - foreign national accounts subject to conditions.
Restrictions: TIN required; Republic's non-resident foreign currency account targets those living abroad; foreign currency scarcity and USD account approvals reported.
Alternatives (fintech / regional): Wise, Revolut; remittance services.
Cost note: Republic Bank (Guyana) savings minimums are cited from GYD 5,000 (about USD 24 at GYD 209/USD) up to GYD 100,000 depending on product; opening and monthly fees are not published.

Documents required: Passport, proof of address, proof of income or employment, foreign bank reference letter, sometimes residence permit and tax ID.
Minimum deposit & fees: Not published; non-residents may face higher opening capital or minimum balances for USD/EUR accounts.
Banks accepting non-residents: De Surinaamsche Bank, Hakrinbank, Republic Bank Suriname (branch visit; no confirmed remote non-resident onboarding).
Restrictions: FX shortages and post-2020 currency crisis, slow onboarding (reports of up to months), correspondent banking limits.
Alternatives (fintech / regional): Wise or Revolut held abroad; Mercury/US fintech for business needs.
Cost note: No published non-resident figures for DSB, Hakrinbank or Republic Bank Suriname; opening capital and minimum balances for USD/EUR accounts are set case by case.

Documents required: Passport, CPF tax number (obtainable from abroad via consulate/Receita Federal), proof of foreign address, foreign TIN, source of funds.
Minimum deposit & fees: Non-resident (CNR) account fees are high at premium banks, e.g. one guide quotes BTG Pactual at about BRL 24,000 a year; others not published.
Banks accepting non-residents: Exchange-authorised banks offering the Conta de Nao Residente (CNR), e.g. BTG Pactual; mainstream retail banks rarely open for non-residents.
Restrictions: Non-residents must use the CNR regime regulated by Banco Central do Brasil; retail banks generally require a residence permit (CRNM); annual CPF re-registration reported for non-residents.
Alternatives (fintech / regional): Wise (PIX-enabled transfers), Nomad or similar USD accounts for Brazilians; law-firm assisted remote onboarding.
Cost note: BTG Pactual non-resident (CNR) account reportedly costs about BRL 24,000 a year (BRL 2,000/month, about USD 370 at BRL 5.4/USD) per a third-party guide; opening fee and minimum deposit are not published, so null.

Documents required: Paraguayan cedula (national ID) normally required, plus passport, local address, proof of income and source-of-funds/patrimony declaration.
Minimum deposit & fees: not published
Banks accepting non-residents: none known for passport-only non-residents; Banco Atlas and Banco Continental require a cedula for full personal accounts.
Restrictions: Since 2026 banks require origin-of-funds and patrimony declarations; tourists generally rejected; non-residents can usually bank only via a Paraguayan company with an RUC.
Alternatives (fintech / regional): Obtain residency and cedula first; otherwise Wise or Revolut from abroad.
Cost note: Not applicable: passport-only non-residents cannot open personal accounts (Banco Atlas and Banco Continental require a cedula), so no costs apply.

Documents required: Passport, proof of foreign address, bank reference letter, proof of income and source of funds; some private banks also want a local tax ID and Uruguayan phone.
Minimum deposit & fees: BROU reportedly requires new non-resident foreigners to place a USD 5,000 fixed-term deposit for 181 days; Santander non-resident accounts carry high minimum balances (amount not published).
Banks accepting non-residents: Banco Republica (BROU), Itau Uruguay (non-resident account), Santander Uruguay (online non-resident account), Scotiabank (in person).
Restrictions: No capital controls and USD accounts widely available; strict source-of-funds checks and CRS/FATCA reporting; non-resident accounts may face higher fees.
Alternatives (fintech / regional): Wise, Revolut; Prex and Mi Dinero cards for locals with cedula.
Cost note: BROU non-resident foreigner page: USD 5,000 fixed-term deposit for 181 days, client registration 300 UI plus savings-account opening 150 UI (450 UI, about UYU 2,900) and a non-waivable monthly fee of 150 UI (about UYU 960), at roughly UYU 6.4 per UI and UYU 40 = USD 1.

Documents required: Passport, Argentine tax ID (CUIT/CUIL; CUIT replaced CDI for foreigners from March 2026), local proof of address; DNI needed for full product range and online banking.
Minimum deposit & fees: Basic accounts (caja de ahorro / cuenta para migrantes at public banks) are free; other fees not published for non-residents.
Banks accepting non-residents: Banco de la Nación Argentina and other public banks (mandated basic accounts); private banks case-by-case.
Restrictions: Many branches refuse passport-only applicants; non-residents face tighter product limits; FX rules eased from April 2025 but still evolving; FATCA/CRS reporting.
Alternatives (fintech / regional): Wise, Western Union, crypto/USDT apps commonly used; local wallets such as Mercado Pago generally require DNI.
Cost note: Banco de la Nacion Argentina basic savings account (caja de ahorros) is free to open and maintain under BCRA basic-account rules (ARS 0); no minimum deposit figure is published for non-residents, so that field is null.

Documents required: Chilean ID card (cedula de extranjeria) with RUT, visa/residence, proof of local address and often local income.
Minimum deposit & fees: CuentaRUT has no minimum; checking accounts typically need income around CLP 800,000/month; non-resident fees not published.
Banks accepting non-residents: none known for non-residents; BancoEstado CuentaRUT and Scotiabank foreigner accounts need residence/visa.
Restrictions: RUT and Chilean ID required; banks generally cannot open accounts from abroad for non-residents.
Alternatives (fintech / regional): Brokerage accounts (high minimums), Wise/Revolut, foreign cards.
Cost note: Non-residents cannot open personal accounts here (CuentaRUT and foreigner accounts need a RUT and residence/visa), so no costs apply.

Documents required: Passport (notarised, apostilled copy for remote opening), proof of foreign address, bank reference letter, photo; in-branch opening needs passport only at many banks.
Minimum deposit & fees: Not published.
Banks accepting non-residents: Golomt Bank (remote savings account for people abroad), Khan Bank, TDB (Trade and Development Bank), XacBank (in-branch).
Restrictions: No legal bar on non-residents; remote opening limited to specific products and slow; FATF grey-list exit in 2023 but enhanced due diligence remains.
Alternatives (fintech / regional): Wise for MNT transfers; QPay/SocialPay need a local account.
Cost note: Golomt, Khan Bank, TDB and XacBank publish no non-resident account fees or minimum deposit (MNT about 3,400/USD), so all figures are unpublished.

Documents required: Residence card (zairyu card), registered Japanese address, Japanese phone number, hanko or signature.
Minimum deposit & fees: Not published; ordinary accounts usually free.
Banks accepting non-residents: none known for non-residents (Japan Post Bank, Rakuten, Shinsei/SBI serve residence-card holders).
Restrictions: Under the FX Act foreigners in Japan under 6 months are non-residents; tourists cannot open accounts and non-resident yen accounts are heavily restricted.
Alternatives (fintech / regional): Wise JPY account details for receiving funds.
Cost note: Non-residents cannot open personal accounts here, so all cost fields are null; ordinary accounts for residence-card holders are usually free.

Documents required: Passport, Korean mobile number in own name, proof of purpose (employment/enrolment) and local address; ARC needed for full services.
Minimum deposit & fees: No minimum deposit typically; fees not published.
Banks accepting non-residents: KB Kookmin, Hana Bank, Shinhan, Woori (in branch, mainly for visitors with a clear Korea connection).
Restrictions: Accounts without an ARC are often teller-only with no ATM, online banking or overseas transfer for months; must open in person in Korea; anti-fraud limits on new accounts.
Alternatives (fintech / regional): Wise, Revolut; for travellers, prepaid cards such as WOWPASS.
Cost note: Major Korean banks (KB Kookmin, Hana, Shinhan, Woori) typically need no minimum deposit; opening and monthly fees for non-resident accounts are not published.

Documents required: Passport with valid visa or visa-free entry stamp, Chinese mobile number, local address, stated purpose of account; many branches still ask for residence permit or temporary residence registration.
Minimum deposit & fees: Typically no or very low minimum (around CNY 10 card fee); some guides cite USD 500 for a USD account at Bank of China.
Banks accepting non-residents: Bank of China, ICBC, Bank of Beijing and other large banks (branch-dependent acceptance of short-term visitors).
Restrictions: Strict capital controls (USD 50,000 annual FX quota), branch discretion, no remote opening for non-residents; tourist-visa applicants often refused.
Alternatives (fintech / regional): Alipay and WeChat Pay linked to foreign cards (PBOC 2024 easing); Wise, Revolut abroad.
Cost note: Large banks such as Bank of China and ICBC typically require no minimum for a CNY debit account and charge about CNY 10 for the card (about USD 1.40 at CNY 7.1/USD); some guides cite USD 500 for a USD account, and monthly fees for visitors are not published.

Documents required: Passport plus secondary ID, a Taiwan Record of ID Number or UBN from the National Immigration Agency, local address and phone; most banks require an ARC.
Minimum deposit & fees: Small NTD opening deposits typical (often around NTD 1,000); non-resident fees not published.
Banks accepting non-residents: none known that routinely accept non-residents; some private banks open passport-only accounts at branch discretion.
Restrictions: FSC rules treat the ARC as the key ID; without it acceptance is at bank discretion and accounts may be restricted to limited functions; foreign-currency accounts and FX limits apply.
Alternatives (fintech / regional): Wise for TWD transfers; keep home-country account; offshore banking units (OBU) for some foreign clients.
Cost note: Typical small NTD opening deposit of about TWD 1,000 (about USD 32 at TWD 31/USD) at banks that accept passport-only clients at branch discretion; opening and monthly fees for non-residents are not published, so null.

Documents required: Passport, proof of foreign residential address, proof of income/source of funds, purpose of account; some banks also ask for tax residency (CRS) self-certification and an in-person visit.
Minimum deposit & fees: HSBC One charges non-HKID holders HKD 100/month below HKD 10,000 balance (from Jan 2026); Premier requires a high balance (not published here); other banks not published.
Banks accepting non-residents: HSBC Hong Kong (international/remote onboarding for residents of designated countries; existing Premier clients qualify automatically); other banks case-by-case.
Restrictions: No capital controls and HKD/USD freely available, but strict AML/KYC; virtual banks generally require a HKID; many banks require a branch visit and reject non-residents without clear HK nexus.
Alternatives (fintech / regional): Wise or Revolut HKD details; Statrys/Airwallex for business only.
Cost note: HSBC One charges non-HKID holders HKD 100/month when the balance is below HKD 10,000 (about USD 1,280) at roughly 0.128 USD/HKD; no opening fee or opening minimum is published.

Documents required: Passport, proof of foreign address, proof of income/source of funds, account purpose; some banks ask for a Macau non-resident worker (Blue) card.
Minimum deposit & fees: not published
Banks accepting non-residents: Bank of China Macau, BNU (Banco Nacional Ultramarino), ICBC Macau; acceptance of non-residents varies by bank and branch.
Restrictions: No legal bar on foreigners, but in-person visit is required and banks apply strict AML due to the gaming sector; MOP pegged to HKD, no capital controls.
Alternatives (fintech / regional): Wise or Revolut; Hong Kong banks for a nearby multi-currency option.
Cost note: Bank of China Macau, BNU and ICBC Macau do not publish non-resident personal account opening fees, minimum deposits or monthly fees, so all figures are null.

Documents required: Passport, proof of foreign residential address (within 3 months), tax residency/TIN declaration, sometimes source-of-funds or reference; Singapore pass needed for digital (Singpass) opening.
Minimum deposit & fees: Non-resident accounts often need higher deposits (roughly up to S$5,000 or more at priority tiers); e.g. DBS Multiplier S$3,000 average balance or S$5 monthly fee.
Banks accepting non-residents: DBS, OCBC, UOB, Citibank Singapore, Standard Chartered, HSBC Singapore (case-by-case, often via priority/wealth tiers).
Restrictions: Strict MAS AML/KYC; many retail products require a pass or local address; non-residents frequently asked to visit a branch in person; CRS/FATCA reporting.
Alternatives (fintech / regional): Wise and Revolut provide SGD local account details; YouTrip and other wallets for spending.
Cost note: DBS Multiplier: no initial deposit required, S$5 monthly fall-below fee if average daily balance is under S$3,000 (about USD 2,310) at ~1.30 SGD/USD; no opening fee is published, and non-resident approval is case-by-case.

Documents required: Passport with valid long-term pass (employment, student, MM2H), proof of address, reference letter; tourist visas generally not accepted.
Minimum deposit & fees: Typically about MYR 250-1,000 for savings/current accounts; non-resident fees not published.
Banks accepting non-residents: Maybank and CIMB cited as foreigner-friendly; HSBC/Standard Chartered premier tiers case-by-case.
Restrictions: Non-residents fall under BNM foreign exchange policy as External Accounts; first account must be opened in branch.
Alternatives (fintech / regional): Wise (may require pass), e-wallets for visitors, international private banking in Labuan.
Cost note: Maybank/CIMB savings accounts reported at about MYR 250 minimum (up to MYR 1,000 for current accounts; USD 1 = MYR 4.2), with non-resident opening and monthly fees not published (web search budget exhausted in pass 2, so figures come from the existing min_deposit_fees text and were not re-verified against a bank tariff).

Documents required: Passport with valid visa; KITAS/KITAP, local address, NPWP tax number and Indonesian phone usually required for full accounts.
Minimum deposit & fees: Tourist-type accounts reportedly require USD 2,000-50,000 balance with higher fees under USD 10,000; otherwise not published.
Banks accepting non-residents: BCA, Bank Mandiri, BNI, BRI, CIMB Niaga (passport-only accounts case-by-case at branches).
Restrictions: Without KITAS most banks refuse; tourist accounts are savings-only with limits; remote opening from abroad not permitted.
Alternatives (fintech / regional): Wise, Revolut; Jenius/digital banks need KTP or KITAS.
Cost note: Tourist-type accounts at banks such as BCA or Mandiri reportedly need a USD 2,000-50,000 balance (IDR about 16,500/USD), with higher fees under USD 10,000; opening and monthly fees are not published.

Documents required: Passport with visa, often a work permit or long-term visa, immigration residence certificate or embassy letter, Thai phone number.
Minimum deposit & fees: UOB non-resident accounts reportedly need THB 50,000; others small or not published.
Banks accepting non-residents: Bangkok Bank, Kasikorn, SCB, UOB (branch discretion; tourists sometimes accepted).
Restrictions: Bank of Thailand rules on non-resident baht accounts and anti-fraud tightening; practice varies by branch.
Alternatives (fintech / regional): Wise THB details; DTV/long-stay visa first.
Cost note: Bangkok Bank FCD savings account for non-residents (fee schedule effective 1 Oct 2018): USD 1,000 initial deposit, USD 10/month charged only if the average balance falls below USD 250 (so 0 if maintained); no opening fee is published.

Documents required: Passport with valid Vietnamese visa or temporary residence card, local address and phone, work permit or labour contract for many banks.
Minimum deposit & fees: Not published; usually low or none at major banks.
Banks accepting non-residents: None known for true non-residents; foreign residents use Vietcombank, Techcombank, HSBC Vietnam, Shinhan Vietnam.
Restrictions: Payment-account rules (Circular 17/2024/TT-NHNN) tie foreigners' accounts to visa/residence validity; savings and foreign-currency deposits by non-residents restricted; biometric verification required.
Alternatives (fintech / regional): Wise, Revolut (no local VND details); foreign portfolio investors use special indirect investment capital accounts.
Cost note: Non-residents cannot realistically open a personal account here, so no cost figures apply (all null).

Documents required: Passport, second ID (often ACR I-Card), proof of local address, Philippine mobile number, sometimes reference or proof of income.
Minimum deposit & fees: BDO about PHP 5,000 and BPI about PHP 3,000 for peso savings; USD accounts often require higher deposits; fees not published for non-residents.
Banks accepting non-residents: BDO, BPI, Metrobank (case-by-case; non-residents mostly limited to USD/EUR foreign-currency deposit accounts).
Restrictions: BSP KYC rules, ACR I-Card requirement effectively excludes short-term visitors, peso accounts often unavailable to non-residents.
Alternatives (fintech / regional): Wise or Revolut for PHP; local e-wallets GCash and Maya need local ID/number.
Cost note: BPI peso savings minimum is about PHP 3,000 (about USD 52 at PHP 58/USD; BDO about PHP 5,000 = USD 86); opening and monthly fees for non-residents are not published.

Documents required: Passport (valid 3+ months), passport photo, proof of foreign address; branch openings usually want a long-term visa extension and lease; remote ACLEDA forms must be notarised and embassy-certified or confirmed by SWIFT MT999.
Minimum deposit & fees: ABA reported at about USD 50 for non-residents; ACLEDA current accounts about USD 1,000; fees low.
Banks accepting non-residents: ACLEDA Bank (overseas account opening), ABA Bank and Canadia Bank (in-branch with visa).
Restrictions: Most banks require a valid stay extension; USD widely used; remote-opened accounts may be limited to email/phone banking until a local SIM is obtained.
Alternatives (fintech / regional): Wise for transfers; Bakong/KHQR wallets need local accounts; Wing and other mobile money mainly for residents.
Cost note: ACLEDA Bank standard savings account lists no opening fee, no initial deposit, no minimum balance and no monthly fee (USD-denominated; statements beyond two months cost USD 2/month), though ABA reportedly asks non-residents for about USD 50 and ACLEDA current accounts about USD 1,000.

Documents required: Passport with valid Lao visa, proof of local address in Laos; work permit for some products such as BCEL i-Bank; source-of-funds for investors.
Minimum deposit & fees: not published; foreign-investor accounts may require USD 10,000 where ministries or the bank require it.
Banks accepting non-residents: BCEL (Banque pour le Commerce Exterieur Lao) is most cited for foreigners; others not confirmed.
Restrictions: Bank of Lao PDR rules allow non-resident foreign-currency accounts with a passport, but banks typically want a visa and local address; foreign-currency shortages and exchange controls on kip.
Alternatives (fintech / regional): Wise or Revolut from Australia; cash/remittance services.
Cost note: Not published: BCEL personal-account opening fees, minimum deposit and monthly fees for non-residents are unpublished (the USD 10,000 figure applies only to some foreign-investor accounts).

Documents required: Passport with a valid long-stay visa (3-6 months or more), proof of local address, employer or embassy letter or investment-commission recommendation.
Minimum deposit & fees: Historical minimums of USD 100-1,000 depending on purpose; current figures not published.
Banks accepting non-residents: none known for non-residents; KBZ Bank, CB Bank, AYA Bank serve resident foreigners.
Restrictions: FATF blacklist (call for action), US/EU/Australian sanctions on military-linked banks (MFTB, MICB), currency controls and forced FX conversion, no interest paid to foreigners.
Alternatives (fintech / regional): none practical; foreigners rely on offshore accounts in Thailand or Singapore.
Cost note: Non-residents cannot open personal accounts in Myanmar, so no cost applies (historical resident-foreigner minimums of USD 100-1,000 are not current).

Documents required: Passport with valid entry/employment/student/dependent pass and local proof of address (Brunei licence, utility bill or employer letter) for standard accounts.
Minimum deposit & fees: Baiduri savings account minimum opening deposit BND 100; non-resident terms not published.
Banks accepting non-residents: Baiduri Bank and BIBD (resident-focused; non-resident case-by-case); Standard Chartered Brunei.
Restrictions: No exchange controls and non-resident accounts permitted by law, but banks generally want a local pass; US persons face hurdles due to no FATCA IGA.
Alternatives (fintech / regional): Wise or Revolut for transfers; BND is pegged 1:1 to SGD so Singapore accounts are a practical substitute.
Cost note: Baiduri Bank savings account minimum opening deposit BND 100 at ~1.30 BND/USD (about USD 77); opening and monthly fees for non-residents are not published.

Documents required: Passport, proof of address, visa or residence documentation, and source of funds; banks follow BCTL KYC instructions.
Minimum deposit & fees: not published
Banks accepting non-residents: BNU (CGD group), ANZ Timor-Leste, BNCTL, Bank Mandiri branch.
Restrictions: Small USD-based banking sector; strict identification under BCTL instructions; non-resident acceptance is case-by-case.
Alternatives (fintech / regional): Keep Australian bank account; Wise/Revolut; ANZ group relationship from Australia.
Cost note: BNU, ANZ, BNCTL and Mandiri publish no non-resident opening fee, minimum deposit or monthly fee (USD is the local currency) (web search budget exhausted in pass 2, so figures come from the existing min_deposit_fees text and were not re-verified against a bank tariff).

Documents required: Passport, visa grant and expected arrival date for migrant accounts; ID verified in branch after arrival; TFN recommended (founder's home country, so this is the inbound-migrant view).
Minimum deposit & fees: Everyday accounts generally have no minimum deposit and no monthly fee for new migrants; interest without TFN taxed at 47%.
Banks accepting non-residents: Commonwealth Bank (apply up to 14 days pre-arrival), Westpac (up to 12 months), ANZ; NAB generally in-branch.
Restrictions: Pre-arrival accounts are deposit-only until in-person ID check in Australia; non-visa-holding non-residents without arrival plans generally cannot open everyday accounts.
Alternatives (fintech / regional): Wise or Revolut Australia offer AUD details; founder's home country, so domestic accounts already available.
Cost note: CommBank Smart Access has no opening fee or minimum deposit and a AUD 4 monthly fee (about USD 2.60 at AUD 0.66), waived if AUD 2,000+ is deposited each month or the holder is under 30.

Documents required: Passport, NZ visa (residence/work/student), overseas address, IRD number or home tax declaration.
Minimum deposit & fees: Not published; standard accounts typically low or no fee.
Banks accepting non-residents: ASB, ANZ, BNZ, Kiwibank (pre-arrival accounts for migrants).
Restrictions: Pre-arrival accounts are limited until in-branch ID verification; programs aimed at people moving with a visa.
Alternatives (fintech / regional): Wise NZD account details.
Cost note: ASB everyday/Streamline account carries NZD 0 monthly fee with electronic statements per third-party migrant guides (not confirmed on ASB's tariff); opening fee and minimum deposit are not published.

Documents required: Passport, Fiji TIN letter (compulsory at BSP), Fiji residential address, proof of address, source of funds.
Minimum deposit & fees: Not published.
Banks accepting non-residents: BSP Fiji, ANZ Fiji, Westpac Fiji (case-by-case; Australian bank ties may help).
Restrictions: Exchange controls by Reserve Bank of Fiji; non-resident and foreign currency accounts governed by residency definitions; TIN requirement hampers non-residents.
Alternatives (fintech / regional): Wise, Revolut; keep funds with Australian parent banks (ANZ, Westpac).
Cost note: Fiji: not published by the banks named and no official tariff could be found, so all three figures are left null.

Documents required: Passport, PNG work permit or visa, local address and employer reference; non-resident accounts require compliance with BPNG FE Manual Notice 11.
Minimum deposit & fees: Not published; BSP foreign-currency accounts carry minimum balances and need BPNG approval.
Banks accepting non-residents: BSP, Kina Bank, ANZ and Westpac PNG operations (non-resident personal accounts not generally offered).
Restrictions: Foreign exchange controls, BPNG approval for FCAs, tax clearance needed for transfers abroad, FX shortages.
Alternatives (fintech / regional): Keep funds in Australia (ANZ/Westpac) or use Wise; local mobile money such as MiBank/CellMoni needs PNG presence.
Cost note: Non-resident personal accounts are not generally offered (BSP foreign-currency accounts need BPNG approval), so no applicable costs.

Documents required: Passport, proof of foreign address, bank reference and source of funds; in-person branch visit.
Minimum deposit & fees: ANZ Samoa foreign-currency accounts for non-residents require a minimum of 200 units (e.g. AUD 200 or USD 200); fees not published.
Banks accepting non-residents: ANZ Samoa (foreign-currency accounts for non-resident individuals), BSP Samoa (case-by-case).
Restrictions: Exchange controls administered by the Central Bank of Samoa; non-resident offerings are mainly foreign-currency accounts; tala accounts may be restricted.
Alternatives (fintech / regional): Wise or remittance services for WST; Digicel/Vodafone mobile money for residents.
Cost note: ANZ Samoa foreign-currency account for non-resident individuals requires a minimum of 200 units (USD 200 used; AUD 200 would be about USD 132 at AUD 1 = USD 0.66); opening and monthly fees are not published, so null.

Documents required: Passport, proof of local physical address (PO Box not accepted), residence or work permit usually expected, plus AML/CFT source-of-funds information.
Minimum deposit & fees: Guides cite about TOP 100-300 opening deposit for a standard account; fees not published.
Banks accepting non-residents: ANZ Tonga, BSP Tonga, Tonga Development Bank (non-resident policy not published).
Restrictions: Small market with AML/CFT de-risking; non-residents face significant challenges and banks prefer a branch visit in Nuku'alofa.
Alternatives (fintech / regional): Wise or Revolut; Australian or NZ bank accounts with remittance to Tonga.
Cost note: Guides cite about TOP 100-300 opening deposit for a standard account at ANZ/BSP Tonga, low end TOP 100 at about 0.42 USD/TOP; opening and monthly fees are not published.

Documents required: Passport, proof of foreign address, bank reference, source-of-funds evidence, completed application taken to a branch.
Minimum deposit & fees: not published
Banks accepting non-residents: ANZ Vanuatu, BRED Bank Vanuatu, Bank South Pacific (BSP) Vanuatu, National Bank of Vanuatu; non-resident acceptance case-by-case.
Restrictions: Formerly on EU/FATF grey lists, causing correspondent de-risking; banks restrict non-residents tied to the citizenship-by-investment programme.
Alternatives (fintech / regional): Wise or Revolut; Australian or NZ bank account for regional transfers.
Cost note: ANZ, BRED, BSP and National Bank of Vanuatu do not publish non-resident personal account opening fees, minimum deposits or monthly fees, so all figures are null.

Documents required: Passport and visa/permit documentation, proof of address, source of funds and references; in-branch identification.
Minimum deposit & fees: Not published.
Banks accepting non-residents: ANZ Solomon Islands, BSP Solomon Islands, Bank of South Pacific; non-resident personal accounts case-by-case.
Restrictions: Central Bank of Solomon Islands exchange controls; foreign-currency accounts need central bank approval; withholding tax on non-resident interest; strict PEP rules.
Alternatives (fintech / regional): Wise/Revolut from Australia for transfers; mobile money services limited.
Cost note: No bank named publishes a non-resident personal tariff (ANZ and BSP Solomon Islands handle non-residents case-by-case), so all three figures are left null as unpublished.

Documents required: Passport and identification per ANZ terms, residential address, likely purpose of account and local connection.
Minimum deposit & fees: ANZ foreign currency account fee USD 5/month; other fees per ANZ Kiribati schedule; minimum deposit not published.
Banks accepting non-residents: ANZ Bank (Kiribati) Limited, Development Bank of Kiribati.
Restrictions: Foreign currency accounts subject to the Exchange Control Ordinance; very small market with limited non-resident service.
Alternatives (fintech / regional): Keep Australian bank (AUD is legal tender); Wise; remittance services.
Cost note: ANZ Kiribati foreign currency account fee of USD 5/month, with opening fee and minimum deposit not published (AUD is the local currency) (web search budget exhausted in pass 2, so figures come from the existing min_deposit_fees text and were not re-verified against a bank tariff).

Documents required: No published non-resident process; CBA accounts opened via e-form for Nauruans and residents.
Minimum deposit & fees: Not published.
Banks accepting non-residents: Commonwealth Bank of Australia (in-country service since August 2025, replacing the Bendigo Bank agency); no domestic bank.
Restrictions: Nauru uses AUD and has no locally licensed bank; CBA service targets Nauruan residents; realistic option for non-residents is an Australian account.
Alternatives (fintech / regional): An Australian bank account (AUD is legal tender); Wise.
Cost note: Non-residents cannot open personal accounts here, so no opening fee, deposit or monthly fee applies.

Documents required: Passport, local Funafuti address, visa or work permit (reported).
Minimum deposit & fees: Reported about AUD 50 minimum deposit (unverified).
Banks accepting non-residents: National Bank of Tuvalu (only commercial bank).
Restrictions: No central bank; uses AUD; correspondent banking ties to Australia at risk per IMF; in-person only.
Alternatives (fintech / regional): Keep Australian bank accounts (AUD is legal tender).
Cost note: Non-residents cannot open personal accounts here, so all cost fields are null; National Bank of Tuvalu reportedly asks about AUD 50 (~USD 33 at 0.66) minimum deposit from residents (unverified).

Documents required: Passport, bank reference, proof of address and a clear local connection; requirements not published.
Minimum deposit & fees: Not published.
Banks accepting non-residents: Bank of the Marshall Islands (domestic; non-resident personal accounts rare).
Restrictions: Tiny sector reliant on a single correspondent relationship; strong de-risking; offshore IBCs barred from local accounts; USD is local currency.
Alternatives (fintech / regional): Wise or Revolut USD details; US bank accounts.
Cost note: Non-residents cannot realistically open a personal account here, so no cost figures apply (all null).

Documents required: Passport, proof of address, likely local address or reference and reason for account; requirements not published.
Minimum deposit & fees: not published
Banks accepting non-residents: Bank of the FSM (only locally incorporated commercial bank); Bank of Guam branches (requirements not published).
Restrictions: USD economy; small market with limited correspondent banking; FATCA/US banking rules apply via US-linked banks.
Alternatives (fintech / regional): Use US or Australian accounts and Wise; Bank of Guam and US online banks if eligible.
Cost note: Bank of the FSM and Bank of Guam do not publish non-resident opening fees, deposits or monthly charges.

Documents required: Passport (translated/notarised if needed), Turkish tax number (vergi numarasi, obtainable from abroad or at a tax office), proof of address (home-country utility bill), Turkish phone number.
Minimum deposit & fees: not published; some non-resident routes reportedly require around USD 6,000 held for three months.
Banks accepting non-residents: Ziraat Bankasi, VakifBank, Garanti BBVA, QNB, HSBC Turkey and Kuveyt Turk reported to accept some non-residents, varying by branch.
Restrictions: Many banks increasingly require a residence permit (ID number starting with 99) and have tightened foreigner onboarding; strict AML checks; lira volatility and FX deposit rules.
Alternatives (fintech / regional): Wise or Revolut for TRY transfers; Papara-type e-money wallets mostly need Turkish ID.
Cost note: Some non-resident routes at Turkish banks reportedly require about USD 6,000 held for three months (reported, not from a bank tariff); opening and monthly fees for non-resident personal accounts are not published, so null.

Documents required: Passport, sometimes proof of foreign address and source-of-funds documents; remote opening usually via notarised/apostilled power of attorney.
Minimum deposit & fees: Low; no significant minimum deposit at retail banks, small annual service fees (not published here); intermediary POA services cost extra.
Banks accepting non-residents: TBC Bank, Bank of Georgia, Liberty Bank, Space Bank (app onboarding for some nationalities).
Restrictions: No legal bar on foreigners but KYC tightened in 2026 with source-of-funds checks; some nationalities restricted; multi-currency GEL/USD/EUR accounts allowed.
Alternatives (fintech / regional): Wise or Revolut; Space Bank app (TBC) for eligible nationalities.
Cost note: Bank of Georgia Basic package: free current-account opening, no stated minimum balance, GEL 5/month for non-residents (GEL 2 for residents) at about 0.37 USD/GEL.

Documents required: Passport (sometimes notarized Armenian translation), local or temporary address, phone number; occasionally purpose of account or source-of-funds proof.
Minimum deposit & fees: Opening often free to about AMD 10,000; monthly fees not published.
Banks accepting non-residents: Ameriabank, Ardshinbank, ACBA Bank, Inecobank, Evocabank; most require a first in-person identification for foreign non-residents.
Restrictions: Enhanced due diligence for some nationalities (notably post-2022 Russian inflows); banks do not use IBAN; sanctions screening.
Alternatives (fintech / regional): Wise or Revolut; Armenian bank mobile apps once onboarded.
Cost note: Armenian banks such as Ameriabank (which advertises a free Smart account) typically open personal accounts free or for up to about AMD 10,000 (about USD 26 at AMD 390 = USD 1); minimum deposits and monthly fees for non-residents are not published.

Documents required: Passport (with notarised Azerbaijani translation if needed); some banks also request local registration, residence permit or tax ID.
Minimum deposit & fees: Not published.
Banks accepting non-residents: Kapital Bank (Birbank) and ABB reportedly open accounts for non-residents with passport at a branch; policies vary.
Restrictions: Central Bank currency regulations allow non-resident accounts in AZN and FX, but banks apply own residence-permit rules; remote onboarding requires ASAN Imza e-signature; CRS reporting.
Alternatives (fintech / regional): Wise and Revolut for transfers; few local fintechs open to non-residents.
Cost note: No bank named publishes a non-resident personal tariff (Kapital Bank and ABB branch openings with passport), so all three figures are left null as unpublished.

Documents required: Passport, IIN (obtained in person at a public service centre), Kazakh phone number, document showing legal basis of stay (entry stamp/visa), home TIN for CRS.
Minimum deposit & fees: Basic card accounts generally free to open; premium tiers higher; specific non-resident fees not published.
Banks accepting non-residents: Kaspi Bank, Halyk Bank, Bank CenterCredit, ForteBank, Freedom Bank.
Restrictions: Remote opening closed since 2025; non-resident cards valid max 12 months; sanctions-related scrutiny for Russian flows; CRS reporting.
Alternatives (fintech / regional): Freedom Finance brokerage, Wise, Revolut.
Cost note: Kaspi Gold basic card account is free to open with no minimum balance and no monthly service fee (KZT, about 520 per USD); premium tiers cost more and non-resident-specific fees are not published (web search budget exhausted in pass 2, so figures come from the existing min_deposit_fees text and were not re-verified against a bank tariff).

Documents required: Passport, temporary registration (hotel or passport office), PINFL personal ID number, Uzbek mobile number; some banks ask non-resident questionnaire and source of funds.
Minimum deposit & fees: Not published; cards often free or low cost.
Banks accepting non-residents: TBC Bank Uzbekistan (app plus courier in Tashkent), Ipak Yo'li Bank, KDB Bank Uzbekistan, Asia Alliance Bank, Kapitalbank.
Restrictions: Must be physically in Uzbekistan with temporary registration; currency conversion controls largely liberalised but non-resident account rules apply.
Alternatives (fintech / regional): Wise to UZS cards; local wallets Payme/Click once a card is held.
Cost note: TBC Bank Uzbekistan and Kapitalbank publish no non-resident opening fee, deposit or monthly fee (UZS about 12,500/USD); cards are said to be free or low cost, but no figure is published.

Documents required: Passport, visa/registration, local presence; banks may refuse at discretion.
Minimum deposit & fees: not published
Banks accepting non-residents: none known (state banks such as Senagat, Dayhanbank, State Bank for Foreign Economic Affairs).
Restrictions: State-owned banking, strict currency controls, separate TMT and USD/EUR accounts, foreigners rarely onboarded.
Alternatives (fintech / regional): none
Cost note: Non-residents cannot open personal accounts here, so all cost fields are null; state banks publish no tariff for foreigners.

Documents required: Passport, Tajik TIN, proof of legal stay (visa/registration); foreign documents may need legalisation at a Tajik mission.
Minimum deposit & fees: Not published.
Banks accepting non-residents: Spitamen Bank (states services for residents and non-residents), Amonatbank (requires proof of legal stay).
Restrictions: Physical presence expected; currency controls on somoni; correspondent banking constraints and Russia-related sanctions spillover affect transfers.
Alternatives (fintech / regional): Wise, Revolut (no local details); money transfer systems such as Western Union.
Cost note: Tajikistan: not published by the banks named and no official tariff could be found, so all three figures are left null.

Documents required: Passport (notarised translation sometimes), client questionnaire, signature card, source-of-funds explanation; local phone helpful.
Minimum deposit & fees: Low or no minimum deposit at most banks; card fees modest; exact non-resident fees not published.
Banks accepting non-residents: Bakai Bank, Optima Bank, Demir Bank, Kicb (non-residents accepted with branch visit or notarised power of attorney).
Restrictions: Heightened scrutiny and EU/US secondary-sanctions concerns over Russia-linked flows; some banks restrict USD transfers.
Alternatives (fintech / regional): Remote opening via notarised power of attorney through intermediaries; Wise; local e-wallets (MBank) need visit.
Cost note: Bakai Bank's individual accounts page states account opening has no service fee and no monthly fee (only transactions are charged); its minimum deposit is not published (KICB reportedly charges KGS 100, about USD 1.15 at KGS 87.4/USD, to open).

Documents required: Passport with valid visa, in-person application; bank-specific forms.
Minimum deposit & fees: not published
Banks accepting non-residents: none known for routine non-resident onboarding; a 2017 Central Bank of Iran directive allows commercial banks to open rial accounts for foreigners in person.
Restrictions: Comprehensive US/EU/UN-related sanctions and FATF blacklist status; Iranian banks are cut off from SWIFT and international cards; Australian sanctions also apply; foreign cards do not work in Iran.
Alternatives (fintech / regional): Tourist prepaid debit cards (e.g. Mah Card/tourist cards) loaded with cash in Iran; cash USD/EUR; no access via Wise or Revolut.
Cost note: Iranian banks may open rial accounts for foreigners in person under a 2017 central bank directive, but no fees or minimum deposits are published and sanctions block routine use, so all three are null.

Documents required: Cameroonian residence permit, taxpayer card (NIU), passport, proof of local address; non-resident accounts mainly for legal entities.
Minimum deposit & fees: not published
Banks accepting non-residents: none known for non-resident individuals.
Restrictions: BEAC/CEMAC foreign-exchange regulation controls non-resident and foreign-currency accounts tightly; residence is the first condition for foreigners per local lawyers.
Alternatives (fintech / regional): Mobile money (MTN MoMo, Orange Money) needs a local SIM and ID; Wise/Revolut from abroad.
Cost note: Not applicable: no known bank opens personal accounts for non-resident individuals, so no costs apply.

Documents required: Biometric passport or consular card plus valid residence card, proof of local address, initial deposit; in-branch opening in Bangui only.
Minimum deposit & fees: not published
Banks accepting non-residents: none known for non-residents; Ecobank Centrafrique, BSIC Centrafrique, Banque Populaire Maroco-Centrafricaine serve residents.
Restrictions: Conflict and security risk; CEMAC/BEAC foreign-exchange regulations restrict foreign-currency accounts; correspondent de-risking; UN arms embargo and sanctions on individuals.
Alternatives (fintech / regional): Orange Money or Moov mobile money with local SIM; Cameroon-based CEMAC banks.
Cost note: Non-residents cannot open personal accounts in the Central African Republic, so no cost applies and none is published.

Documents required: Passport with valid visa or residence card, accommodation certificate, proof of earnings (Chad-specific Ecobank requirement), notarised copies for non-residents.
Minimum deposit & fees: Not published.
Banks accepting non-residents: Ecobank Tchad (non-resident accounts subject to local regulation, branch visit expected); no bank known to routinely open for non-residents.
Restrictions: CEMAC/BEAC foreign-exchange regulation tightly controls foreign-currency and non-resident accounts; XAF-to-FX conversions need justification; high AML scrutiny and de-risking.
Alternatives (fintech / regional): Mobile money (Airtel Money, Moov Money) requires local SIM/ID; foreigners generally rely on home-country accounts and remittance services.
Cost note: Non-residents cannot realistically open a personal account here, so no opening fee, minimum deposit or monthly fee applies or is published.

Documents required: Passport (6+ months validity), visa or residence permit, proof of Congolese address (lease, utility bill or accommodation certificate), TIN if available, initial deposit.
Minimum deposit & fees: not published
Banks accepting non-residents: Societe Generale Congo, BGFIBank Congo, BCI (Banque Commerciale Internationale) cited by guides; non-residents rated difficult.
Restrictions: CEMAC/BEAC foreign exchange regulation restricts transfers out of the zone; heavy KYC for non-residents; XAF accounts.
Alternatives (fintech / regional): Mobile money (MTN MoMo, Airtel Money) needs local SIM/ID; Wise/foreign bank accounts.
Cost note: Societe Generale, BGFIBank and BCI Congo publish no non-resident opening fee, minimum deposit or monthly fee (web search budget exhausted in pass 2, so figures come from the existing min_deposit_fees text and were not re-verified against a bank tariff).

Documents required: Passport with visa, proof of address (foreign and often local host attestation), completed opening forms including FATCA/CRS self-certification; residence card often requested.
Minimum deposit & fees: No opening fee typically, but banks require a minimum balance; amounts not published.
Banks accepting non-residents: Rawbank, Equity BCDC, Ecobank RDC, Access Bank RDC, TMB (in-branch identity check required).
Restrictions: Economy heavily dollarised (USD and CDF accounts); conflict in the east, enhanced AML scrutiny (FATF grey list) and correspondent de-risking; no remote opening for non-residents found.
Alternatives (fintech / regional): Mobile money (M-Pesa Vodacom, Orange Money, Airtel Money) with local SIM and ID; Wise does not pay out locally.
Cost note: Banks such as Rawbank and Equity BCDC typically charge no opening fee but require a minimum balance; the balance and monthly fees are not published (accounts usually in USD).

Documents required: Passport, proof of address, residence permit if any, tax ID if available, initial deposit.
Minimum deposit & fees: not published
Banks accepting non-residents: BGFIBank Gabon, Ecobank, UBA (non-residents finalise at branch or via power of attorney).
Restrictions: CEMAC/BEAC exchange rules; non-resident foreign-currency accounts allowed but cannot go overdrawn.
Alternatives (fintech / regional): Mobile money (Airtel Money, Moov Money) needs local SIM; Wise for sending.
Cost note: BGFIBank, Ecobank and UBA Gabon do not publish non-resident opening deposits or account-keeping fees, and the tariff could not be retrieved this pass, so all figures are null.

Documents required: Passport, residence permit, local proof of address, tax number and initial deposit.
Minimum deposit & fees: Not published.
Banks accepting non-residents: None known for non-residents; local banks include BANGE, Societe Generale Equatorial Guinea, CCEI Bank GE, Ecobank.
Restrictions: CEMAC/BEAC exchange controls (2018 regulation) tightly restrict foreign-currency accounts and transfers; heavy AML scrutiny.
Alternatives (fintech / regional): Wise, Revolut not locally available; use home-country accounts and money transfer services.
Cost note: Non-residents cannot realistically open a personal account here, so no cost figures apply (all null).

Documents required: Passport, proof of address, tax number (NIF) and likely residence permit or local justification; requirements not published.
Minimum deposit & fees: not published
Banks accepting non-residents: Banco Internacional de Sao Tome e Principe (BISTP), majority-owned by CGD; acceptance of non-residents unconfirmed.
Restrictions: Central bank controls on foreign-exchange operations, slow correspondent transfers, STN pegged to EUR.
Alternatives (fintech / regional): Portuguese banks (CGD, BPI) with non-resident accounts; Wise or Revolut.
Cost note: BISTP does not publish fees or minimum deposits, and acceptance of non-residents is unconfirmed.

Documents required: Passport, passport-size photo, proof of address; source-of-funds information for foreign-currency accounts.
Minimum deposit & fees: not published
Banks accepting non-residents: Bank of Kigali (personal current accounts open to non-Rwandans in RWF, USD, EUR, GBP and others); remote diaspora accounts are for Rwandans.
Restrictions: KYC requires in-person verification at a branch for foreigners; National Bank of Rwanda AML rules apply.
Alternatives (fintech / regional): MTN MoMo and Airtel Money mobile money (need local SIM registration); Wise transfers to RWF.
Cost note: Bank of Kigali personal current accounts are open to non-Rwandans, but no opening fee, minimum deposit or monthly fee was found in a published tariff, so all three are null.

Documents required: Passport, residence permit, proof of local address or residence registration, employment/assignment letter, TIN if available.
Minimum deposit & fees: Initial deposit varies by bank; not published.
Banks accepting non-residents: none known for non-residents; CRDB Bank Burundi, BANCOBU, BCB and KCB Burundi require branch KYC.
Restrictions: Visitor visa not sufficient; strict foreign-exchange controls and chronic USD shortages; diaspora accounts limited to Burundian nationals.
Alternatives (fintech / regional): Mobile money (Lumicash, Ecocash) requires local SIM/ID; Wise/Revolut from abroad.
Cost note: Not applicable: non-residents cannot open accounts remotely (branch KYC required at CRDB, BANCOBU, BCB, KCB), and initial deposits are not published.

Documents required: Passport plus long-term visa, work permit or residence certificate at most banks; local address, TIN for some accounts, passport photos.
Minimum deposit & fees: not published
Banks accepting non-residents: Stanbic Bank Uganda, Absa Bank Uganda, Standard Chartered Uganda; foreigners with only a short-term visa are commonly refused.
Restrictions: Bank of Uganda KYC rules tie accounts to lawful stay; remote diaspora accounts are for Ugandan nationals only; FX accounts in USD available.
Alternatives (fintech / regional): MTN MoMo or Airtel Money with a registered SIM (needs passport and visa); Wise or Revolut for transfers.
Cost note: Stanbic, Absa and Standard Chartered Uganda do not publish non-resident personal account costs, and short-term visitors are commonly refused, so all figures are null.

Documents required: Passport, visa or residence/work permit (bank-dependent), proof of address, two photos, TRA TIN (non-residents can apply online), opening deposit.
Minimum deposit & fees: Not published.
Banks accepting non-residents: CRDB Bank, NMB Bank, Stanbic, Standard Chartered Tanzania (permit usually requested; case-by-case for non-residents).
Restrictions: Foreign Exchange Regulations 2022 allow residents and non-residents to hold FX accounts locally; many banks still demand a permit; strict KYC.
Alternatives (fintech / regional): Mobile money (M-Pesa, Tigo Pesa/Mixx, Airtel Money) needs local SIM registered with NIDA or passport; Wise transfers into TZS.
Cost note: No bank named publishes a non-resident personal tariff (CRDB, NMB, Stanbic and Standard Chartered usually request a permit), so all three figures are left null as unpublished.

Documents required: Passport, KRA PIN (or KRA private ruling exemption), local referee/introducer, proof of address, passport photos.
Minimum deposit & fees: not published
Banks accepting non-residents: Diamond Trust Bank and Standard Chartered reported anecdotally; Equity and KCB diaspora accounts target Kenyans.
Restrictions: KRA PIN required for any account; each bank sets its own non-resident policy; diaspora products mostly for Kenyan nationals.
Alternatives (fintech / regional): M-Pesa (needs Kenyan SIM registered with passport), Wise, Revolut.
Cost note: DTB and Standard Chartered Kenya publish no non-resident terms, and diaspora accounts target Kenyans (web search budget exhausted in pass 2, so figures come from the existing min_deposit_fees text and were not re-verified against a bank tariff).

Documents required: Passport, proof of address, proof of source of funds, sometimes a professional reference letter; residence permit if applicable.
Minimum deposit & fees: Reportedly around KMF 10,000 for some local accounts; otherwise not published.
Banks accepting non-residents: BIC Comores (Banque pour l'Industrie et le Commerce), Exim Bank Comores, Banque de Développement des Comores (case-by-case, in person).
Restrictions: Small cash-based banking system with scarce ATMs; KMF pegged to the euro under French Treasury arrangement; no published non-resident process.
Alternatives (fintech / regional): Wise or Revolut held abroad; local mobile money requires a Comorian SIM and ID.
Cost note: Some local accounts at BIC Comores reportedly need about KMF 10,000 (about USD 24 at KMF 420/USD); opening and monthly fees are not published.

Documents required: Passport, residence or investor status, landlord attestation, JIRAMA utility bill, photos.
Minimum deposit & fees: BNI reportedly MGA 400,000 minimum deposit (old forum report).
Banks accepting non-residents: none known for non-residents (BNI, BOA, BFV/Societe Generale Madagasikara, BMOI serve residents).
Restrictions: Foreigners need established residence or investor status; physical presence required; French-language service.
Alternatives (fintech / regional): Mobile money (MVola, Orange Money) with local SIM.
Cost note: Non-residents cannot open personal accounts here, so all cost fields are null; BNI reportedly required MGA 400,000 (~USD 90 at 4,500/USD) minimum deposit from residents per an old forum report.

Documents required: Passport, reference letter, proof of residence, ZRA TPIN, proof of income; many banks also want a work or study permit.
Minimum deposit & fees: Not published.
Banks accepting non-residents: Stanbic Bank Zambia, Zanaco, Absa Zambia, FNB Zambia (mostly require permits; case-by-case for non-residents).
Restrictions: Banks typically ask for a Zambian permit and local address; foreign-currency accounts available but subject to AML checks.
Alternatives (fintech / regional): Wise, mobile money (MTN MoMo, Airtel Money) once locally registered.
Cost note: Zambia: not published by the banks named and no official tariff could be found, so all three figures are left null.

Documents required: Passport, residence or work permit, local address, KYC forms; FCDA requires a Kwacha operating account.
Minimum deposit & fees: not published
