Banks accepting non-residents: National Bank of Malawi, Standard Bank Malawi (FCDA eligibility limited to exporters, NGOs, Malawians abroad).
Restrictions: Exchange controls, 2024 regulations on FCDAs and mandatory conversion, chronic FX shortages.
Alternatives (fintech / regional): Wise or Revolut abroad; mobile money (Airtel Money, TNM Mpamba) needs local SIM and ID.
Cost note: Non-residents cannot open personal accounts (FCDA eligibility limited to exporters, NGOs and Malawians abroad), so no applicable costs.

Documents required: Passport with signed non-resident declaration, NUIT tax number, income statement or work contract, reference letter from home bank; foreign documents notarised, legalised by Mozambican consulate and in Portuguese.
Minimum deposit & fees: First Capital Bank minimum deposit about MZN 1,000; others not published.
Banks accepting non-residents: Millennium bim (published non-resident document list); First Capital Bank case-by-case.
Restrictions: Bank of Mozambique foreign-exchange controls; foreign-currency accounts require justification such as service contracts; documents must be in Portuguese.
Alternatives (fintech / regional): M-Pesa (Vodacom) and e-Mola mobile money with local SIM; Wise transfers not widely supported to MZN.
Cost note: First Capital Bank minimum deposit of about MZN 1,000 (about USD 16 at MZN 64/USD); opening and monthly fees at First Capital Bank and Millennium bim for non-residents are not published, so null.

Documents required: Passport with work or residence visa or resident card, Angolan tax number (NIF), proof of address; investors need BNA-regulated investor account documentation.
Minimum deposit & fees: not published
Banks accepting non-residents: none known for ordinary non-resident individuals; non-resident investor accounts possible at local commercial banks.
Restrictions: Non-resident kwanza accounts are regulated foreign-exchange operations under BNA rules (Notice 1/23); visa required for foreigners; FX controls and USD scarcity.
Alternatives (fintech / regional): Wise/Revolut from abroad; Unitel Money/e-Kwanza require local ID.
Cost note: Not applicable: ordinary non-resident individuals cannot open personal accounts, and no fees are published.

Documents required: Certified passport, work or residence permit, Botswana proof of residence (utility bill), proof of income; non-resident files case-by-case.
Minimum deposit & fees: Absa Botswana personal accounts cite minimum income of BWP 750; non-resident deposits/fees not published.
Banks accepting non-residents: Absa Bank Botswana, FNB Botswana, Stanbic Bank Botswana, Standard Chartered Botswana, First Capital Bank; none confirmed to onboard non-residents remotely.
Restrictions: No exchange controls (abolished 1999) and foreign-currency accounts available, but strict KYC tied to local residence.
Alternatives (fintech / regional): Orange Money or MyZaka mobile money with local SIM; South African bank non-resident accounts; Wise or Revolut.
Cost note: Absa Botswana cites a minimum income of BWP 750 (about USD 55 at BWP 13.6 = USD 1), which is an eligibility test not a deposit; no Botswana bank publishes non-resident opening, deposit or monthly fees.

Documents required: Passport with visa endorsement, proof of foreign address, source of funds; in-person FICA verification or notarised documents couriered to the branch.
Minimum deposit & fees: Not published.
Banks accepting non-residents: FNB Namibia (non-resident foreign currency accounts), Bank Windhoek (non-resident accounts with notarised remote route reported).
Restrictions: Common Monetary Area exchange controls administered by Bank of Namibia; non-resident accounts flagged and FX flows reported; FIA AML/KYC requirements.
Alternatives (fintech / regional): Wise transfers to NAD; South African bank non-resident accounts usable within the CMA.
Cost note: No bank named publishes a non-resident personal tariff (FNB Namibia and Bank Windhoek non-resident accounts), so all three figures are left null as unpublished.

Documents required: Certified passport/ID copy, proof of foreign residence (lease, utility bill, bank statement or affidavit), passport photo, application form.
Minimum deposit & fees: Steward Bank non-resident FCA: USD 20 opening deposit and USD 5 service fee; others not published.
Banks accepting non-residents: Steward Bank (non-resident FCA via diaspora banking); other banks case-by-case.
Restrictions: RBZ exchange controls; non-resident FCAs in USD; currency export limits and customs declarations; history of currency instability.
Alternatives (fintech / regional): EcoCash mobile money (local SIM), Wise/remittance services to Zimbabwe.
Cost note: Steward Bank non-resident FCA with a USD 20 opening deposit and a USD 5 service fee, assumed monthly, while the opening fee is not published (web search budget exhausted in pass 2, so figures come from the existing min_deposit_fees text and were not re-verified against a bank tariff).

Documents required: Passport, proof of local residence, residence or work permit, tax number; in-branch verification.
Minimum deposit & fees: Not published.
Banks accepting non-residents: None known for non-residents; Standard Bank Eswatini, FNB Eswatini, Nedbank Eswatini and Eswatini Bank serve residents and permit holders.
Restrictions: Common Monetary Area exchange controls classify non-CMA persons as non-residents; banks require permits; practical workaround is a South African non-resident account usable across the CMA.
Alternatives (fintech / regional): Standard Bank South Africa non-resident account (opened remotely, ZAR usable in Eswatini); Wise; MTN MoMo with local SIM.
Cost note: Non-residents cannot open personal accounts here, so no opening fee, deposit or monthly fee applies.

Documents required: Passport or work permit, proof of residential address, source of funds, employment/income proof, tax details.
Minimum deposit & fees: not published
Banks accepting non-residents: none known for non-residents (Standard Lesotho Bank Pro tier open to foreigners with full KYC).
Restrictions: Common Monetary Area with South Africa; KYC assumes local address; Standard Bank SA excludes Lesotho residents from its non-resident accounts.
Alternatives (fintech / regional): South African bank accounts; M-Pesa/EcoCash with local SIM.
Cost note: Non-residents cannot open personal accounts here, so all cost fields are null; Standard Lesotho Bank tariffs apply only to customers with full local KYC.

Documents required: Certified passport copy, foreign proof of address (under 3 months), 3 months of foreign bank statements, proof of income, signed bank forms.
Minimum deposit & fees: Standard Bank non-resident account fees per its pricing guide; 0.60% fee on outward payments outside the CMA; minimum deposit not published.
Banks accepting non-residents: Standard Bank (dedicated non-resident account, applications by email), FNB, Absa, Nedbank.
Restrictions: Exchange control (SARB) rules apply to non-resident rand accounts; FICA KYC; limited credit products for non-residents.
Alternatives (fintech / regional): Wise ZAR, Revolut; TymeBank/Discovery mainly for residents.
Cost note: Standard Bank's 2026 Non-Residents Pricing Guide was found but its account monthly fee and minimum deposit could not be extracted (it lists outward payments outside the CMA at 0.783%, min ZAR 295.65, max ZAR 991.30, about USD 17-57 at ZAR 17.5/USD), so all three are null.

Documents required: Passport, proof of foreign address, foreign TIN, reason or tie to the Netherlands; BSN and Dutch address usually required within 90 days at retail banks.
Minimum deposit & fees: No minimum deposit; ABN AMRO charges a monthly non-resident surcharge on top of standard account fees (higher tier for Australia).
Banks accepting non-residents: ABN AMRO (non-residents with a Dutch link, surcharge applies); ING and bunq require EEA residence or Dutch address.
Restrictions: Strict AML/KYC, de-risking of non-EEA residents (ABN AMRO closed ~15,000 non-EEA accounts), CRS reporting.
Alternatives (fintech / regional): Wise, Revolut or bunq for EUR IBAN; N26 or other EU neobanks if EEA-resident.
Cost note: ABN AMRO charges no opening fee or minimum deposit, but its January 2026 non-resident surcharge puts Australia in category 2 at EUR 8.00 per account per month (about USD 9.40 at USD 1.17/EUR), on top of the regular payment-package fee which is not included here.

Documents required: Passport, proof of foreign address, foreign TIN, source-of-funds evidence and reason for a Belgian account; online opening generally requires Belgian residence or itsme/eID.
Minimum deposit & fees: Basic banking service about EUR 1.60/month at BNP Paribas Fortis (EU residents only); non-resident current-account fees not published.
Banks accepting non-residents: BNP Paribas Fortis (non-resident clients handled at designated branches, case-by-case); other banks discretionary.
Restrictions: Statutory basic-account right covers only EU legal residents and certain Belgians abroad; banks may refuse non-EU residents for AML reasons; CRS reporting.
Alternatives (fintech / regional): Wise or Revolut (Belgian/Lithuanian IBAN available to many non-residents), N26 for EEA residents.
Cost note: BNP Paribas Fortis basic banking service of about EUR 1.60/month applies to EU residents only, and non-resident current-account fees are not published, so all three are null.

Documents required: Passport, proof of foreign address (certificate of residence or utility bill under 3 months), proof of income; some banks want a Luxembourg employment contract or payslips.
Minimum deposit & fees: Retail accounts have small monthly package fees (not published here); private banks typically require high minimum assets (not published).
Banks accepting non-residents: Spuerkeess (BCEE) explicitly accepts non-residents incl. digital onboarding; BGL BNP Paribas partially digital; private banks for wealthier clients.
Restrictions: Some banks serve only residents or cross-border workers; digital onboarding excluded for AML/compliance flags; EU AML and CRS reporting to ATO.
Alternatives (fintech / regional): Wise, Revolut (EUR IBAN) without residency.
Cost note: Spuerkeess Zebra package is EUR 3.50/month (EUR 42/year, fee information document dated April 2024) at about 1.15 USD/EUR; no opening fee or minimum deposit is published there.

Documents required: Passport, proof of foreign address, proof of income, foreign tax identification number; some banks require an existing EU/French IBAN for the first deposit.
Minimum deposit & fees: Non-resident accounts often carry higher monthly fees and minimum deposits; amounts not published consistently.
Banks accepting non-residents: BNP Paribas (non-resident/expat service), Societe Generale (branch discretion), CIC and Credit Agricole regional banks for property buyers; Boursobank is mostly resident-only.
Restrictions: No capital controls; CRS/FATCA reporting; non-resident accounts usually lack overdrafts and credit; Banque de France 'droit au compte' covers residents of France (and certain EU cases) only.
Alternatives (fintech / regional): N26, Revolut, bunq or Wise for EUR IBANs opened remotely.
Cost note: BNP Paribas, Societe Generale and regional banks charge non-residents higher monthly fees and deposits but do not publish consistent non-resident amounts, so all figures are null.

Documents required: Passport, proof of foreign home address, proof of income/source of funds, tax ID (TIN) declaration; traditional banks often want a Meldebescheinigung; notarised copies if opening remotely.
Minimum deposit & fees: Not published for non-residents; standard current accounts typically cost a few EUR per month.
Banks accepting non-residents: Deutsche Bank, Commerzbank, Sparkassen case-by-case in branch; online banks N26 and bunq require a German/EEA address.
Restrictions: Basic payment account right (Basiskonto) covers persons legally resident in the EU, not non-EU non-residents; strict GwG KYC; CRS/FATCA reporting.
Alternatives (fintech / regional): Wise and Revolut offer EUR IBANs to Australian residents; N26/bunq need EEA residence.
Cost note: Deutsche Bank, Commerzbank and Sparkassen open non-resident accounts case-by-case with no published non-resident tariff (standard current accounts cost a few EUR per month), so figures are left null as unpublished.

Documents required: Passport, proof of address (Meldezettel usually requested; foreign address may be accepted case-by-case), TIN/CRS self-certification, proof of income/source of funds.
Minimum deposit & fees: Typical current accounts cost roughly EUR 3-10/month; non-resident terms not published.
Banks accepting non-residents: Erste Bank (branch only for non-residents per guides); others case-by-case.
Restrictions: Online onboarding (e.g. George) restricted to Austrian residents; EU basic account right covers EU legal residents only; strict AML and CRS reporting.
Alternatives (fintech / regional): N26, Revolut, Wise (EUR IBAN; eligibility depends on residence).
Cost note: Erste Bank-type current accounts cost roughly EUR 3-10/month, low end shown (EUR 1 = USD 1.17), with non-resident opening fee and minimum deposit not published (web search budget exhausted in pass 2, so figures come from the existing min_deposit_fees text and were not re-verified against a bank tariff).

Documents required: Passport, proof of foreign address, foreign tax ID (CRS), source-of-wealth and income evidence; video identification accepted by Swiss regulation.
Minimum deposit & fees: Swissquote reportedly requires a first deposit of about CHF/EUR 500; private banks often require CHF 100,000+; non-resident account fees generally higher.
Banks accepting non-residents: Swissquote and Dukascopy Bank (remote onboarding for many countries); UBS and cantonal/private banks for higher-balance clients.
Restrictions: No banking secrecy for tax (CRS/AEOI with Australia); many retail banks refuse foreign domiciles or US persons; bank-specific excluded-country lists.
Alternatives (fintech / regional): Wise, Revolut; Yuh and Neon are limited to Swiss/EU residents.
Cost note: Swissquote's official fee pages list no opening fee and charge custody fees (CHF 20-50 per quarter) only on securities, not cash, while its first deposit is reported at about CHF 500 (about USD 625 at CHF 1.25/USD); non-Swiss tax statements cost CHF 100.

Documents required: Passport, proof of address, bank reference, detailed source-of-wealth and source-of-funds documentation, tax self-certification.
Minimum deposit & fees: Reported CHF 100,000-500,000 at LLB and around CHF/EUR 1 million at LGT or VP Bank (unverified).
Banks accepting non-residents: LGT, Liechtensteinische Landesbank (LLB), VP Bank.
Restrictions: Private-banking model with high minimums; CRS/FATCA reporting; US persons restricted.
Alternatives (fintech / regional): Swiss private banks; Wise CHF/EUR accounts.
Cost note: Minimum is the low end of the reported (unverified) CHF 100,000-500,000 at LLB converted at ~1.25 USD/CHF (LGT/VP Bank reportedly ~CHF/EUR 1 million); opening and monthly fees are not published.

Documents required: Two government IDs, proof of foreign address, detailed source of wealth and income, bank references; in-person meeting usually required.
Minimum deposit & fees: Private banking for non-residents typically EUR 500,000 to EUR 2-3 million; standard accounts cited at EUR 10,000-50,000.
Banks accepting non-residents: CFM Indosuez, Compagnie Monegasque de Banque, Barclays Monaco, UBS Monaco, Societe Generale Private Banking Monaco.
Restrictions: Accounts effectively private-banking only for non-residents; French residents often refused; intensive AML and CRS reporting.
Alternatives (fintech / regional): Wise, Revolut (EU IBANs); French or Luxembourg banks.
Cost note: Minimum deposit is the low end of the EUR 10,000-50,000 cited for standard non-resident accounts (about USD 11,700 at USD 1.17/EUR; private banking needs EUR 500,000+); opening and monthly fees are not published.

Documents required: Passport, proof of foreign address, source-of-funds documentation, tax ID for CRS.
Minimum deposit & fees: Reported EUR 500-2,000 opening deposit depending on bank; fees not published.
Banks accepting non-residents: Banca di San Marino, Cassa di Risparmio della Repubblica di San Marino, Banca Agricola Commerciale (private-banking style, case-by-case).
Restrictions: CRS participant, enhanced AML after past grey-listing, account restrictions may apply initially for new non-resident clients.
Alternatives (fintech / regional): Italian or other EU banks; Wise, Revolut.
Cost note: Reported opening deposits are EUR 500-2,000 depending on bank (lower bound EUR 500, about USD 585 at USD 1.17/EUR); opening and monthly fees are not published.

Documents required: Passport, proof of foreign address, recent bank statements, home-country tax return, source-of-funds and source-of-wealth evidence.
Minimum deposit & fees: Reported opening deposits range from EUR 0-5,000 at some banks, but non-resident offerings are often private banking with six-figure minimums; Creand reportedly charges about EUR 200 to open and EUR 220 per semester.
Banks accepting non-residents: Andbank, Creand Credit Andorra, MoraBanc, Vall Banc (non-resident accounts case-by-case).
Restrictions: Strict AML and source-of-funds checks; CRS automatic exchange with Australia; accounts in EUR; onboarding takes weeks.
Alternatives (fintech / regional): Wise or Revolut for EUR; Spanish or French banks nearby.
Cost note: Creand Credit Andorra reportedly charges about EUR 200 to open (about USD 232) and EUR 220 per semester (about EUR 37/month, about USD 43) at EUR 1 = USD 1.16; the minimum deposit for non-residents is not published (reported EUR 0-5,000, often six figures for private banking), so null.

Documents required: Passport; often a PESEL number (obtainable for tax purposes), proof of foreign address, sometimes tax residence certificate; branch visit or video verification.
Minimum deposit & fees: Basic accounts often free or low monthly fee (around PLN 0-10, varies by bank); not published for non-residents specifically.
Banks accepting non-residents: PKO Bank Polski, mBank, Bank Millennium, Santander Bank Polska, Bank Pekao (practice varies).
Restrictions: Many banks insist on PESEL and branch visit; EU AML checks and CRS reporting; no capital controls.
Alternatives (fintech / regional): Wise, Revolut (Polish-licensed EU bank) with PL IBAN.
Cost note: Not published for non-residents: basic personal accounts at PKO BP, mBank and others run about PLN 0-10/month (about USD 0-2.7 at 0.27 USD/PLN), but no bank publishes a specific non-resident tariff.

Documents required: Passport plus second photo ID, for non-EU citizens often a residence permit or proof of Czech connection (lease, employment, study), Czech phone number.
Minimum deposit & fees: Some banks ask for an opening deposit of CZK 100-1,000; non-resident fees not published.
Banks accepting non-residents: Fio banka and Raiffeisenbank sometimes open in branch; Air Bank reportedly no longer opens for foreigners; acceptance case-by-case.
Restrictions: Online opening requires Czech bank ID or residence; banks may refuse non-EU non-residents without local ties; standard EU AML/CRS rules.
Alternatives (fintech / regional): Revolut, Wise, N26 (EUR) and similar EU fintechs.
Cost note: Fio banka advertises its personal account as free (no opening or monthly fee, CZK 0); other banks may ask an opening deposit of CZK 100-1,000 (about USD 4-43 at CZK 23 = USD 1) and a Fio minimum deposit is not published.

Documents required: Passport plus second ID, proof of home-country address, tax residence certificate/TIN, sometimes residence permit; translations may be required.
Minimum deposit & fees: Opening generally free; minimum balance may apply; non-resident fees not published.
Banks accepting non-residents: Tatra banka, Slovenská sporiteľňa, VÚB and ČSOB open accounts for foreigners in branch; app opening requires Slovak/EU residence.
Restrictions: No legal ban on non-resident accounts (EUR and FX allowed), but banks set their own residence rules; EU AML and CRS/FATCA reporting.
Alternatives (fintech / regional): Wise and Revolut provide EUR IBANs usable for SEPA payments.
Cost note: Tatra banka, Slovenska sporitelna, VUB and CSOB generally open accounts free of charge (EUR 0); minimum balances and monthly fees for non-residents are not published, so those are null.

Documents required: Passport; usually residence permit and address card (lakcimkartya) or proof of rental; some banks accept passport only.
Minimum deposit & fees: OTP foreign currency accounts reported with no minimum deposit; other fees not published.
Banks accepting non-residents: OTP Bank and others case-by-case; some banks refuse non-residents by policy.
Restrictions: Physical presence usually required; non-resident accounts may be limited to foreign-currency accounts; CRS reporting.
Alternatives (fintech / regional): Wise, Revolut (EU IBAN).
Cost note: OTP Bank foreign currency account reported with no minimum deposit, with opening and monthly fees not published (HUF about 335 per USD) (web search budget exhausted in pass 2, so figures come from the existing min_deposit_fees text and were not re-verified against a bank tariff).

Documents required: Passport, Slovenian tax number (davčna številka, obtained via form DR-02 from FURS, by mail or in person), foreign tax number and proof of foreign address.
Minimum deposit & fees: Not published; standard account fees typically a few euros per month.
Banks accepting non-residents: NLB, OTP banka, Intesa Sanpaolo Bank (Slovenia), Addiko Bank, Sparkasse (branch opening).
Restrictions: Some banks cap deposits/withdrawals on non-resident accounts; EU AML and CRS reporting apply; online opening generally needs Slovenian e-ID.
Alternatives (fintech / regional): Wise, Revolut, N26 (EU IBANs, for EEA residents).
Cost note: Account packages at NLB, OTP banka and others reportedly cost a few euros a month (EUR 1 = USD 1.16), but no non-resident opening fee, deposit or exact monthly fee is published.

Documents required: Passport and Croatian tax number (OIB, issued at a tax office on presentation of passport); sometimes proof of foreign address.
Minimum deposit & fees: Not published; small or no opening deposit at most banks.
Banks accepting non-residents: PBZ, Zagrebacka banka, Erste, Raiffeisen (RBA), OTP.
Restrictions: Non-resident accounts available with OIB; branch visit usually required; euro area since 2023.
Alternatives (fintech / regional): Wise, Revolut (EUR IBAN).
Cost note: PBZ euro current account fee EUR 1.61/month per its April 2026 tariff for domestic and foreign individuals (first fee charged 90 days after opening; digital banking EUR 1.59/month extra), converted at ~1.16 USD/EUR; no opening fee or minimum deposit is published.

Documents required: Passport, foreign proof of address, court-certified translation of foreign documents, purpose of account; some banks want a CIPS residence certificate.
Minimum deposit & fees: Not published.
Banks accepting non-residents: Raiffeisen Bank BiH (non-resident accounts under FBiH rulebook), UniCredit Bank BiH, Intesa Sanpaolo Banka BiH.
Restrictions: Non-resident accounts regulated by entity-level rulebooks; documents must be renewed or account is blocked; KM pegged to EUR.
Alternatives (fintech / regional): Wise, Revolut, Paysera.
Cost note: Bosnia & Herzegovina: not published by the banks named and no official tariff could be found, so all three figures are left null.

Documents required: Passport (with court-interpreter translation where needed), stated purpose of account; sometimes proof of address.
Minimum deposit & fees: No minimum deposit generally; monthly maintenance around EUR 2-10; card issuance fee.
Banks accepting non-residents: Banca Intesa Beograd, Raiffeisen Banka, AIK Banka, OTP Banka Srbija, Unicredit Serbia.
Restrictions: No remote opening for non-residents; non-residents can hold dinar and FX accounts; CRS reporting; scrutiny of Russia-linked flows.
Alternatives (fintech / regional): Authorised representative with power of attorney; Wise, Revolut.
Cost note: Banca Intesa Beograd's individuals' tariff (May 2024) lists RSD 220 per month for a non-resident dinar payment account (about USD 2.20 at RSD 100/USD) with no minimum deposit; a separate opening fee is not published and card issuance is charged extra.

Documents required: Passport (original and copy), proof of address, 6-12 months of bank statements, source of income, evidence of economic ties to Montenegro (e.g. property ownership).
Minimum deposit & fees: not published
Banks accepting non-residents: CKB (Crnogorska Komercijalna Banka) and other banks case-by-case with proof of local ties.
Restrictions: Banks require a strong basis such as property or business ties; some nationalities restricted; branch visit required; EUR-denominated.
Alternatives (fintech / regional): Wise or Revolut for EUR; banks in neighbouring EU states.
Cost note: CKB and other Montenegrin banks consider non-residents case-by-case and publish no non-resident opening fee, minimum deposit or monthly fee, so all three are null.

Documents required: Valid foreign passport (or EU/Schengen ID), completed application, source-of-funds information; power of attorney signed abroad must be apostilled.
Minimum deposit & fees: Small monthly maintenance fees; exact non-resident tariffs not published here.
Banks accepting non-residents: Komercijalna Banka Skopje (published non-resident conditions); other banks such as Stopanska Banka case-by-case.
Restrictions: Non-resident accounts are FX current accounts (with MKD use permitted) under National Bank rules; remote opening generally unavailable; enhanced due diligence on origin of funds.
Alternatives (fintech / regional): Wise or Revolut from abroad.
Cost note: Not published: Komercijalna Banka's non-resident general conditions refer to its tariff without giving opening, minimum-balance or monthly amounts.

Documents required: Passport, proof of foreign address, stated purpose of account; some banks want apostilled documents or an Albanian residence permit.
Minimum deposit & fees: not published
Banks accepting non-residents: Credins Bank (in-branch KYC with passport), Raiffeisen Bank Albania (online only for residents), BKT; policies vary by branch.
Restrictions: Albania removed from FATF grey list in 2023 but banks remain cautious; several banks refuse non-Albanians without residence permit.
Alternatives (fintech / regional): Wise or Revolut; Albanian residence permit route for full banking.
Cost note: Credins, Raiffeisen Albania and BKT do not publish non-resident personal account opening fees, minimum deposits or monthly fees, so all figures are null.

Documents required: Passport, Moldovan fiscal code from the State Tax Service (obtained first), proof of foreign address, source-of-funds information; a representative with power of attorney may act.
Minimum deposit & fees: Not published.
Banks accepting non-residents: maib, Moldindconbank, Victoriabank, OTP Bank Moldova, ProCredit Bank (stricter).
Restrictions: Law 62/2008 lets non-residents open accounts without restriction, but Law 308/2017 AML means enhanced due diligence for non-residents; CRS reporting.
Alternatives (fintech / regional): Wise and Revolut for transfers; local e-wallets require Moldovan ID.
Cost note: maib, Moldindconbank, Victoriabank and OTP Moldova do not publish a non-resident personal account tariff that could be found (only legal-entity schedules), so all three are null as unpublished.

Documents required: Passport (often with notarised Ukrainian translation), tax registration number (RNOKPP), and in practice usually a residence permit.
Minimum deposit & fees: not published
Banks accepting non-residents: none known reliably; PrivatBank and others reported to require residence permits in practice.
Restrictions: Martial law since 2022 with NBU currency controls and cross-border transfer limits; non-resident current accounts legally allowed since 2019 but banks often refuse.
Alternatives (fintech / regional): Wise, Revolut, foreign bank accounts.
Cost note: No bank reliably opens accounts for non-residents without a residence permit, and no non-resident fees are published (web search budget exhausted in pass 2, so figures come from the existing min_deposit_fees text and were not re-verified against a bank tariff).

Documents required: Passport with notarised Russian or Belarusian translation, proof of legal stay (visa/registration) at some banks, local phone number for SMS codes.
Minimum deposit & fees: Reported large frozen minimum balances for non-resident foreign-currency accounts at some banks (e.g. Priorbank); not officially published.
Banks accepting non-residents: Priorbank, Belarusbank, Belagroprombank (in person or via notarised power of attorney).
Restrictions: Currency law allows non-resident accounts but banks may refuse; Australian, EU and US sanctions on Belarus and several state banks; restricted SWIFT and foreign-card access.
Alternatives (fintech / regional): None practical for an Australian; Wise and Revolut do not support BYN.
Cost note: Priorbank and others reportedly require large frozen minimum balances on non-resident foreign-currency accounts (BYN about 3.3/USD), but no official amounts are published.

Documents required: Passport, proof of foreign address, possibly Romanian tax ID (CIF/NIF) and source-of-funds info.
Minimum deposit & fees: Reported a few hundred to a few thousand RON depending on bank.
Banks accepting non-residents: BCR, Banca Transilvania, Raiffeisen Bank Romania.
Restrictions: Remote app-based opening mostly aimed at Romanians abroad; foreigners usually visit a branch.
Alternatives (fintech / regional): Revolut, Wise (EUR/RON details).
Cost note: Banca Transilvania's individual fee sheet lists RON 0 monthly administration for a lei current account (resident terms; non-resident tariff not separately published); minimum deposit is only reported vaguely as a few hundred to a few thousand RON, so null.

Documents required: Passport (6+ months validity), Bulgarian address, foreign tax ID, proof of income, sometimes reference letter or criminal record; LNCH helps.
Minimum deposit & fees: KYC/document-review fees reported at EUR 100-500 for non-residents; minimum deposit not published.
Banks accepting non-residents: UniCredit Bulbank, DSK Bank (power of attorney opening possible case-by-case).
Restrictions: Many banks refuse non-EU non-residents without residence permit or D visa; AML/CRS; Bulgaria adopted the euro in 2026.
Alternatives (fintech / regional): Wise, Revolut, Paysera (EU IBANs).
Cost note: Opening fee is the low end of the EUR 100-500 KYC/document-review fees reported for non-residents at UniCredit Bulbank/DSK (about USD 117 at USD 1.17/EUR); minimum deposit and monthly fees are not published.

Documents required: Passport, Greek tax number (AFM, obtainable via tax representative), proof of foreign address, proof of income or employment; translations may be needed.
Minimum deposit & fees: Low or no minimum deposit; monthly fees typically a few euros; non-resident specifics not published.
Banks accepting non-residents: Piraeus Bank (online with video identification, eligibility to be checked), National Bank of Greece, Eurobank, Alpha Bank (usually branch visit).
Restrictions: AFM practically required, CRS reporting, signature may require one in-branch visit; legacy 2015 capital controls now lifted.
Alternatives (fintech / regional): Wise, Revolut or other EU neobanks for EUR IBAN.
Cost note: Greek banks (Piraeus, NBG, Eurobank, Alpha) quote low or no minimums and monthly fees of a few euros for residents, but non-resident figures are not published.

Documents required: Certified passport copy, proof of foreign address (under 3 months), bank reference, CV, income and source-of-wealth documents, foreign TIN.
Minimum deposit & fees: not published
Banks accepting non-residents: Eurobank Cyprus (non-residents case-by-case with enhanced checks); Bank of Cyprus generally prefers residence permit holders.
Restrictions: Heavy post-2013 de-risking and enhanced due diligence for non-residents; CRS reporting; banks may require a clear Cyprus nexus.
Alternatives (fintech / regional): Wise or Revolut for EUR; licensed EMIs based in Cyprus offering IBANs.
Cost note: Eurobank Cyprus and Bank of Cyprus publish no non-resident personal opening fee, minimum deposit or monthly fee, so all three are null.

Documents required: Passport, recent proof of foreign address, bank reference letter, proof of income and source of funds, evidence of ties to Malta and purpose of account.
Minimum deposit & fees: not published; non-Europeans may face higher fees.
Banks accepting non-residents: Bank of Valletta (branch appointment, strict onboarding), HSBC Malta (online start but branch ID check, mainly Malta/EU residents).
Restrictions: Strong de-risking after FATF grey-listing era; 2-8 week processing; non-EU applicants face extra scrutiny and frequent refusals.
Alternatives (fintech / regional): Wise, Revolut (EUR IBAN); Maltese EMIs mainly for business.
Cost note: Not published: Bank of Valletta and HSBC Malta do not publish non-resident opening fees, minimum deposits or monthly fees.

Documents required: Passport plus second ID at some banks, proof of foreign address, all certified by a solicitor or police officer and in English; PPS number not needed for non-residents.
Minimum deposit & fees: not published
Banks accepting non-residents: Bank of Ireland (non-resident account, certified documents by post), AIB (contact form, branch ID check within 30 days); PTSB mostly resident-only.
Restrictions: No capital controls; CRS/FATCA reporting; banks often expect an Irish link such as property purchase; few remaining full-service banks after Ulster Bank and KBC exits.
Alternatives (fintech / regional): Revolut (Irish-licensed bank with IE IBANs for EEA residents), Wise, N26 or bunq.
Cost note: Bank of Ireland and AIB do not publish separate non-resident account opening fees, minimum deposits or maintenance fees in the sources gathered, so all figures are null.

Documents required: Passport, proof of overseas address, proof of income or wealth, tax residency/TIN declaration; certified copies for remote opening.
Minimum deposit & fees: High thresholds: e.g. Lloyds International £50,000 income or £25,000 savings; HSBC Expat from £50,000 balances or £100,000 salary; Barclays International £40/month if balance under £25,000.
Banks accepting non-residents: HSBC Expat, Lloyds Bank International, Barclays International (Jersey/Isle of Man offshore arms); onshore high-street banks require a UK address.
Restrictions: Standard UK current accounts need a UK address; offshore arms covered by Jersey/IoM deposit schemes not FSCS; strict AML and CRS/FATCA reporting.
Alternatives (fintech / regional): Wise and Revolut provide GBP account details to Australian residents; some EMIs offer UK sort codes.
Cost note: Barclays International charges GBP 40 a month if balances are under GBP 25,000, and Lloyds Bank International requires GBP 25,000 savings (or GBP 50,000 income), converted at ~1.33 USD/GBP; no separate opening fee is published.

Documents required: Passport and Icelandic kennitala (or non-resident system ID from Registers Iceland), electronic ID for app onboarding.
Minimum deposit & fees: not published
Banks accepting non-residents: none known for pure non-residents; Arion, Landsbankinn, Islandsbanki require kennitala.
Restrictions: Kennitala required by all banks; non-resident system IDs usually tied to employment or property; no remote onboarding for non-residents.
Alternatives (fintech / regional): Wise, Revolut; foreign cards widely accepted.
Cost note: Non-residents cannot open personal accounts here (Arion, Landsbankinn and Islandsbanki require a kennitala), so no costs apply.

Documents required: Passport, D-number or Norwegian national ID number (needed for BankID), proof of foreign address and purpose; some banks order a D-number for the client.
Minimum deposit & fees: Non-resident accounts often require a large deposit; amounts not published.
Banks accepting non-residents: Some SpareBank 1 banks and local savings banks case-by-case; DNB reportedly stopped non-resident onboarding.
Restrictions: Without a D-number access is often savings-only; BankID needed for online banking; strict AML/CRS checks.
Alternatives (fintech / regional): Wise, Revolut; Vipps requires a Norwegian bank account.
Cost note: SpareBank 1 and local savings banks handle non-residents case by case, often asking for a large deposit (NOK about 10.5/USD), but no amounts are published.

Documents required: Passport, registered Finnish address, residence permit or proof of residence; Finnish ID code not legally required for basic services.
Minimum deposit & fees: Not published; basic accounts carry monthly fees.
Banks accepting non-residents: Nordea, OP, Danske Bank (in practice require Finnish address).
Restrictions: Basic-banking right covers EEA residents; banks usually require a Finnish registered address; strong e-ID not given without Finnish ID.
Alternatives (fintech / regional): Wise, Revolut, or EU online banks.
Cost note: Nordea Finland basic current account EUR 2.60/month from 1 May 2026 (access codes EUR 0.99 and debit card EUR 2.99 extra), converted at ~1.16 USD/EUR; no opening fee or minimum deposit is published.

Documents required: Passport, proof of right of residence or residence permit, often personnummer or coordination number, proof of employment or study.
Minimum deposit & fees: Not published.
Banks accepting non-residents: Handelsbanken, SEB, Swedbank, Nordea (rarely for non-residents; limited service without personnummer).
Restrictions: Without personnummer, BankID and online banking typically unavailable; strict AML; non-EU non-residents usually refused.
Alternatives (fintech / regional): Wise, Revolut, N26 (EU IBANs; no Swedish BankID).
Cost note: Sweden: not published by the banks named and no official tariff could be found, so all three figures are left null.

Documents required: Passport, CPR number (usually required) or foreign TIN at some banks, Danish address, reason for account.
Minimum deposit & fees: not published
Banks accepting non-residents: Nordea (reportedly accepts foreign TIN in place of CPR), Sydbank (case-by-case); Danske Bank generally requires CPR.
Restrictions: Post-Danske Bank scandal AML tightening, strong de-risking of non-residents, MobilePay requires CPR and Danish number.
Alternatives (fintech / regional): Wise, Revolut, Payset or other EMIs offering Danish/EU IBANs.
Cost note: Non-residents generally cannot open personal accounts without a CPR number, so no applicable costs.

Documents required: Passport, proof of foreign address, documents proving a connection to Estonia (property, employment, business, study), source-of-funds evidence; e-Residency card is not accepted as ID.
Minimum deposit & fees: not published for personal accounts; banks charge non-refundable review fees for non-resident business applicants (about EUR 300 at LHV/Swedbank).
Banks accepting non-residents: LHV Pank, Swedbank, SEB (only with demonstrable Estonian connection).
Restrictions: Non-residents cannot be identified digitally at LHV; e-Residency alone is not a basis for an account; tightened AML after the Danske scandal; special rules for Russian/Belarusian citizens.
Alternatives (fintech / regional): Wise, Revolut, Paysera and other EMIs offering EUR IBANs with remote onboarding.
Cost note: LHV, Swedbank and SEB publish no non-resident personal-account fees (the about EUR 300 review fee applies to non-resident business applicants only), so all three are null.

Documents required: Passport, Latvian residence permit or documented connection to Latvia (employment, study, property, business), proof of income and source of funds, tax returns/statements.
Minimum deposit & fees: Non-resident fees can be high; specifics not published.
Banks accepting non-residents: Swedbank, SEB, Citadele (each requires a connection to Latvia for non-residents).
Restrictions: Heavy de-risking of non-resident clients since the ABLV money-laundering cases; remote onboarding only for Latvian ID/eID holders.
Alternatives (fintech / regional): Wise, Revolut, Lithuanian EMIs.
Cost note: Not published: Swedbank, SEB and Citadele levy higher non-resident fees but the specific amounts are not published.

Documents required: Passport, questionnaire on account purpose and Lithuanian connection, income and source-of-funds proof; some banks require a residence permit.
Minimum deposit & fees: Swedbank charges an administration fee for non-EU residents; SEB charges higher monthly fees to non-residents; opening fees reported up to EUR 400.
Banks accepting non-residents: SEB, Swedbank, Luminor, Artea Bankas (formerly Siauliu bankas); acceptance of non-EU non-residents is case-by-case.
Restrictions: Very strict compliance after Baltic money-laundering scandals; banks often refuse non-residents without local ties; sanctions screening for Russia/Belarus links.
Alternatives (fintech / regional): Lithuanian-licensed EMIs and Revolut Bank UAB offer LT IBANs remotely; Wise, Paysera.
Cost note: Swedbank and SEB charge non-EU residents an administration fee and higher monthly fees, with opening fees reported up to EUR 400 (about USD 465 at USD 1.16 = EUR 1), but no bank publishes a definitive non-resident figure, so values are null.

Documents required: Passport, NIE plus certificado de no residente (single procedure since May 2025, via police or consulate), proof of home address, proof of income/source of funds.
Minimum deposit & fees: Not published; non-resident accounts commonly carry monthly maintenance fees.
Banks accepting non-residents: Santander (non-resident online account with passport reported), Banco Sabadell, CaixaBank, BBVA, Bankinter (cuenta de no residente).
Restrictions: Banks must verify non-resident status every two years; Ley 10/2010 AML source-of-funds checks; CRS/FATCA reporting; branch practices vary.
Alternatives (fintech / regional): Wise and Revolut provide EUR IBANs; Spanish neobanks generally require residence.
Cost note: Santander, Sabadell, CaixaBank, BBVA and Bankinter non-resident accounts commonly carry monthly maintenance fees, but no current figure was confirmed from a bank tariff, so all three are null as unpublished.

Documents required: Passport, foreign proof of address, Portuguese NIF (obtainable via fiscal representative), proof of income/source of funds, CRS tax self-certification.
Minimum deposit & fees: Opening deposit around EUR 250 at some banks; intermediary remote packages roughly EUR 270-700; monthly fees vary.
Banks accepting non-residents: Millennium bcp, Caixa Geral de Depositos, Novo Banco, ActivoBank cited by guides.
Restrictions: NIF required first; strict AML and CRS reporting; US persons face FATCA scrutiny.
Alternatives (fintech / regional): Remote-opening intermediaries; Wise, Revolut (EUR IBAN).
Cost note: Opening deposit of about EUR 250 at some banks such as Millennium bcp/CGD (EUR 1 = USD 1.17); the bank opening fee is not published, intermediary remote-opening packages cost about EUR 270-700 (USD 315-820), and monthly fees vary by bank (web search budget exhausted in pass 2, so figures come from the existing min_deposit_fees text and were not re-verified against a bank tariff).

Documents required: Passport, codice fiscale (free from Agenzia delle Entrate or an Italian consulate abroad), proof of foreign address and foreign tax ID.
Minimum deposit & fees: Not published; conto non residenti fees vary by bank, often a monthly fee plus imposta di bollo.
Banks accepting non-residents: Intesa Sanpaolo, UniCredit, BNL BNP Paribas, Banco BPM (conto corrente non residenti, branch visit typically required).
Restrictions: Non-resident accounts may have limited services; EU AML and CRS reporting; requirements vary between branches.
Alternatives (fintech / regional): Wise, Revolut, N26 (EU IBANs, for EEA residents).
Cost note: Intesa Sanpaolo, UniCredit and others charge varying monthly fees plus the EUR 34.20 annual imposta di bollo on non-resident current accounts, but no standard non-resident tariff is published (EUR 1 = USD 1.16).

Documents required: Only eligible categories (Catholic institutions, clergy, Vatican employees/pensioners, diplomats accredited to the Holy See).
Minimum deposit & fees: not published
Banks accepting non-residents: none (the IOR does not accept ordinary foreign individuals).
Restrictions: IOR closed lay accounts that fall outside its categories; residents and visitors use Italian banks in Rome.
Alternatives (fintech / regional): Italian banks or EU fintechs (Wise, Revolut).
Cost note: Non-residents cannot open personal accounts here, so all cost fields are null; the IOR does not accept ordinary foreign individuals.

Documents required: Passport, second ID, foreign proof of address, foreign bank statements, source of funds; FATCA/CRS forms.
Minimum deposit & fees: Not published; monthly account fees apply and vary by bank.
Banks accepting non-residents: Bank Leumi, Bank Hapoalim, Mizrahi-Tefahot, Discount Bank (non-resident accounts common for property buyers).
Restrictions: Usually requires a branch visit or notarised power of attorney; strict AML and source-of-funds checks; FATCA/CRS reporting.
Alternatives (fintech / regional): Wise ILS, Revolut.
Cost note: Monthly fee is Bank Leumi's cheapest paid plan, Digital Leumi at ILS 10/month (plans range ILS 10-35; about USD 2.7 at ILS 3.7/USD), not confirmed for non-resident accounts; opening fee and minimum deposit are not published.

Documents required: Passport, proof of address (utility bill or tenancy contract), often Jordanian residence permit and personal number; source of funds.
Minimum deposit & fees: Ahli Bank current account minimum balance JOD 200; others not published.
Banks accepting non-residents: Housing Bank (HBTF) accepts passports from non-resident non-Jordanians for savings accounts; Ahli Bank and Jordan Islamic Bank require residency.
Restrictions: CBJ AML/KYC rules, most banks require residency for current accounts, no remote opening for foreigners.
Alternatives (fintech / regional): Wise, Revolut; local e-wallets require Jordanian ID or residency.
Cost note: Housing Bank (the bank accepting non-resident passports) does not publish non-resident savings costs; Ahli Bank's JOD 200 current-account minimum (about USD 282 at JOD 0.709/USD) applies only to residents.

Documents required: Passport, proof of address, home-bank references, purpose of account and source-of-funds declaration; branch visit or lawyer with power of attorney.
Minimum deposit & fees: Byblos Bank fresh-money account minimum USD 1,000; other banks not published.
Banks accepting non-residents: Byblos Bank (fresh accounts); BLOM and Bank Audi reported to open fresh accounts case-by-case.
Restrictions: Post-2019 banking crisis with informal capital controls on legacy deposits; only fresh-money accounts are freely usable; FATF grey-listing (2024) and correspondent de-risking; no legal bar on non-residents.
Alternatives (fintech / regional): Cash USD, Whish Money and OMT money transfer services; Wise not supported for LBP payouts.
Cost note: Byblos Bank fresh-money account minimum of USD 1,000 (USD-denominated, no conversion); opening and monthly fees are not published, so null.

Documents required: Passport with Syrian entry/temporary residence stamp, local address, ID copies; in-person visit in Damascus.
Minimum deposit & fees: Cham Bank current account minimum SYP 10,000 or FX equivalent; others not published.
Banks accepting non-residents: none known for remote non-residents; Cham Bank and Bank Audi Syria accept non-Syrians only in person.
Restrictions: US and EU economic sanctions lifted 2025-2026 and SWIFT reconnected Nov 2025, but correspondent banking and USD access remain very limited; liquidity withdrawal limits.
Alternatives (fintech / regional): Realistically bank via Lebanese, Jordanian, Turkish or Gulf banks; Wise/Revolut not available for Syria transfers in most cases.
Cost note: Not applicable: remote non-residents cannot open accounts; Cham Bank's in-person current-account minimum is SYP 10,000 or FX equivalent, a negligible amount at current rates.

Documents required: Passport, Iraqi residency card, salary attestation or employer letter, compliance clearance; in-branch visit required.
Minimum deposit & fees: Varies by bank; Byblos Bank Iraq term deposits from USD 20,000; current-account minimums not published.
Banks accepting non-residents: none known for non-residents; Byblos Bank Iraq, Rafidain and Rasheed (state) and Kurdistan private banks serve residents.
Restrictions: US Federal Reserve-driven USD restrictions and bans on many Iraqi banks for dollar transactions; strict CBI KYC; security risks; cash-heavy economy.
Alternatives (fintech / regional): Zain Cash, Qi Card and FIB (First Iraqi Bank app) need local ID; Western Union for transfers.
Cost note: Non-residents cannot open personal accounts in Iraq, so no cost applies (Byblos Bank Iraq term deposits from USD 20,000 are for eligible residents).

Documents required: Passport plus Iqama for residents; non-residents need either a Visitor ID (from Sept 2025) or written Ministry of Interior/Foreign Affairs approval routed via SAMA.
Minimum deposit & fees: Not published.
Banks accepting non-residents: Major Saudi banks (e.g. Al Rajhi, SNB) under SAMA rules; visitor-account offerings still emerging.
Restrictions: SAMA rule 200.2.3 bars accounts for non-Saudi non-GCC non-residents without ministry approval; visitor accounts reportedly limited in scope; strict AML/KYC.
Alternatives (fintech / regional): Wise transfers to SAR; STC Bank/urpay and other wallets require Iqama or Saudi ID.
Cost note: No bank named publishes a non-resident personal tariff (Al Rajhi and SNB visitor-account offerings are still emerging under SAMA rules), so all three figures are left null as unpublished.

Documents required: Kuwaiti civil ID, residence visa, employer No Objection Certificate, passport, salary certificate.
Minimum deposit & fees: not published
Banks accepting non-residents: none known for non-resident personal accounts; NBK, Gulf Bank, KFH require civil ID.
Restrictions: Personal accounts tied to residency and civil ID; digital onboarding needs civil ID face match; brokerage accounts (e.g. KMEFIC) may accept embassy-attested passports.
Alternatives (fintech / regional): Kuwaiti brokerage accounts; KFH UK subsidiary; Wise/Revolut held abroad.
Cost note: Non-residents cannot open personal accounts here (NBK, Gulf Bank and KFH require a Kuwaiti civil ID), so no costs apply.

Documents required: Passport, entry visa, recent bank statements, source of wealth declaration; most banks require a Qatar ID (QID) and salary certificate.
Minimum deposit & fees: Not published.
Banks accepting non-residents: QNB (non-resident accounts by direct enquiry), other banks case-by-case.
Restrictions: Standard retail accounts are tied to the QID; reported pre-arrival accounts require a QID within 90 days under QCB rules.
Alternatives (fintech / regional): Wise, Revolut.
Cost note: QNB handles non-resident accounts only on direct enquiry and publishes no fees or minimum balance (QAR 3.64/USD peg).

Documents required: Passport with UAE entry stamp, proof of foreign address, 6 months of bank statements, bank reference letter, proof of income/source of funds.
Minimum deposit & fees: Reported AED 3,000-5,000 at Emirates NBD and AED 25,000+ at Mashreq for non-residents; some banks AED 100,000+.
Banks accepting non-residents: Emirates NBD, Mashreq, ADCB, RAKBANK, FAB.
Restrictions: Non-resident accounts usually savings-type with no chequebook or credit; at least one branch visit common; strict AML checks.
Alternatives (fintech / regional): Wise AED details; UAE digital banks require Emirates ID.
Cost note: Emirates NBD current account (Key Fact Statement): AED 3,000 minimum average balance (~USD 817 at 3.6725 AED/USD) with an AED 26.25 (~USD 7.15) monthly fall-below fee only if under that balance, so 0 if maintained; no opening fee is published.

Documents required: Passport, foreign proof of address, bank reference letter, proof of income, photo, initial deposit.
Minimum deposit & fees: Not published.
Banks accepting non-residents: Bank Muscat (dedicated non-resident savings accounts, first account in OMR).
Restrictions: Non-resident products limited to savings accounts at few banks; branch visit required; AML checks.
Alternatives (fintech / regional): Wise, Revolut (no local OMR details).
Cost note: Bank Muscat needs no minimum to open a savings account but charges a monthly ledger fee if the daily balance falls below OMR 100 (about USD 260 at USD 2.60/OMR); the fee amount and any opening fee are not published in the sources found.

Documents required: Passport or national ID, proof of foreign address, bank reference/statements from home country, economic reason for account, source of funds.
Minimum deposit & fees: not published
Banks accepting non-residents: National Bank of Bahrain, Bank ABC (non-resident acceptance case-by-case; most retail banks expect a CPR).
Restrictions: CBB rulebook requires enhanced due diligence and documented acceptance criteria for non-residents; remote e-KYC only for Bahrainis.
Alternatives (fintech / regional): Wise, Revolut; GCC private banking for high-net-worth clients.
Cost note: National Bank of Bahrain and Bank ABC do not publish non-resident personal account fees or minimums.

Documents required: Passport with Yemeni residence/visa and local address; in-person only.
Minimum deposit & fees: not published
Banks accepting non-residents: none known for non-residents.
Restrictions: Civil conflict with a split Central Bank (Aden vs Sanaa), dual currency rates, cash liquidity shortages; US designations of the Houthis and sanctions on Sanaa-based banks; most foreign banks avoid correspondent relationships.
Alternatives (fintech / regional): Hawala and remittance agents (e.g. Al-Kuraimi exchange network); Western Union-type transfers; no fintech access.
Cost note: Non-residents cannot open personal accounts at Yemeni banks, so all three are null.

Documents required: Palestinian or Jerusalem ID typically required, plus residence evidence; foreign companies must be registered with the Companies Registrar.
Minimum deposit & fees: not published
Banks accepting non-residents: none known; Bank of Palestine reportedly requires a Palestinian/Jerusalem ID.
Restrictions: Banking depends on Israeli correspondent arrangements and shekel cash constraints; PMA classifies non-residents strictly; Gaza banking severely disrupted by conflict.
Alternatives (fintech / regional): Jordanian banks (e.g. in Amman) or Israeli banks serve most cross-border needs; local wallets like PalPay need local ID.
Cost note: Not applicable: Bank of Palestine reportedly requires a Palestinian/Jerusalem ID, so non-residents cannot open accounts and no costs apply.

Documents required: Passport with valid entry visa, proof of address, local mobile number, source of funds; many branches still ask for a residence or work permit.
Minimum deposit & fees: Initial cash deposit usually required; amounts vary by bank and are not published for non-residents.
Banks accepting non-residents: National Bank of Egypt, CIB, HSBC Egypt (branch visit with passport and visa); practice varies between branches.
Restrictions: CBE circular of August 2024 requires banks to open non-resident accounts for foreigners, but with full KYC; FX repatriation and withdrawal documentation rules; currency volatility.
Alternatives (fintech / regional): InstaPay and mobile wallets (Vodafone Cash) need a local account or SIM; Wise for transfers.
Cost note: National Bank of Egypt, CIB and HSBC Egypt require an initial cash deposit but do not publish amounts or monthly fees for non-residents, so all figures are null.

Documents required: Local ID/residence documents and in-branch presence; no non-resident onboarding documented.
Minimum deposit & fees: Not published.
Banks accepting non-residents: None known for non-residents; Bank of Khartoum, Omdurman National Bank serve locals and diaspora.
Restrictions: Ongoing civil war since 2023, collapsed correspondent banking and international de-risking, residual US sanctions on individuals and entities, severe FX shortages.
Alternatives (fintech / regional): Bank of Khartoum's Bankak app and exchange houses for diaspora; foreigners use home-country accounts and remittance providers.
Cost note: Non-residents cannot realistically open a personal account here, so no opening fee, minimum deposit or monthly fee applies or is published.

Documents required: Passport and Libyan residence papers; local address and in-branch visit.
Minimum deposit & fees: not published
Banks accepting non-residents: none known for non-residents; Aman Bank, Jumhouria Bank, National Commercial Bank serve residents.
Restrictions: Political division and conflict; Central Bank of Libya FX controls, cash shortages and dual exchange rates; foreigners reported refused locally; heavy de-risking by correspondents.
Alternatives (fintech / regional): Offshore/international accounts; Western Union and MoneyGram transfers with limits.
Cost note: Non-residents cannot open personal accounts here (local banks serve residents only), so no costs apply.

Documents required: Passport, proof of foreign residence; banks may ask for further KYC.
Minimum deposit & fees: Not published; press reports cite DZD 50,000 deposits at some banks for clients without salary domiciliation.
Banks accepting non-residents: Not published; state banks (e.g. BNA, CPA, BEA) and foreign-owned banks such as Société Générale Algérie and BNP Paribas El Djazair offer foreign-currency accounts.
Restrictions: Bank of Algeria Regulation 09-01 allows non-resident foreigners to hold foreign-currency accounts; strict exchange controls, dinar non-convertible, official rate only.
Alternatives (fintech / regional): None practical locally; Wise does not pay out in DZD.
Cost note: Press reports cite DZD 50,000 deposits (about USD 375 at DZD 133/USD) at some banks for clients without salary domiciliation; opening and monthly fees are not published.

Documents required: Passport, sometimes a Tunisian address, declaration of other accounts; customs declaration of imported foreign cash.
Minimum deposit & fees: not published
Banks accepting non-residents: BNA, Amen Bank, STB, ABC Bank, UBCI, Attijari Bank.
Restrictions: Non-residents may freely open foreign-currency or convertible-dinar accounts without BCT approval; ordinary dinar accounts are subject to exchange controls.
Alternatives (fintech / regional): Wise for transfers; few fintech options locally.
Cost note: BNA, Amen Bank, STB and others do not publish a non-resident (convertible dinar) account tariff that could be retrieved this pass, so all figures are null.

Documents required: Passport and proof of foreign residence; banks may request extra KYC documents.
Minimum deposit & fees: Not published.
Banks accepting non-residents: Bank of Africa, Attijariwafa Bank, BMCE/CIH, Societe Generale Maroc (convertible-dirham and foreign-currency accounts).
Restrictions: Non-residents limited to convertible-dirham or foreign-currency accounts funded only from abroad; Office des Changes exchange controls.
Alternatives (fintech / regional): Wise, Revolut (no MAD local details).
Cost note: Morocco: not published by the banks named and no official tariff could be found, so all three figures are left null.

Documents required: Passport, proof of local address, photos, often residence permit; foreign-exchange account needed for transfers.
Minimum deposit & fees: not published
Banks accepting non-residents: Attijari Bank Mauritanie, BMCI, Banque Nationale de Mauritanie (non-resident requirements not published).
Restrictions: Foreign-exchange regulation by Banque Centrale de Mauritanie, limited correspondent access, cash-based economy.
Alternatives (fintech / regional): Wise or Revolut abroad; local mobile wallets (Bankily, Masrvi) need local SIM and ID.
Cost note: Attijari Bank Mauritanie, BMCI and BNM do not publish non-resident personal account fees or minimums.

Documents required: Passport, proof of foreign residence, funding by transfer from abroad, per Moroccan Office des Changes rules for non-resident convertible-dirham accounts.
Minimum deposit & fees: not published
Banks accepting non-residents: Moroccan banks with branches in Laayoune and Dakhla (e.g. Bank of Africa, Attijariwafa, Banque Populaire) under Moroccan regulation; no Sahrawi (SADR) banks.
Restrictions: Disputed territory administered by Morocco; Moroccan exchange controls apply (non-resident convertible-dirham or foreign-currency accounts only); dirham not exportable; very limited banking outside main towns.
Alternatives (fintech / regional): Open a non-resident convertible-dirham account at a Moroccan bank in Rabat/Casablanca; Wise transfers to MAD.
Cost note: Moroccan banks with branches in Laayoune and Dakhla publish no non-resident personal-account fees or minimum deposits for this territory, so all three are null.

Documents required: Residence or work permit for foreigners; diaspora FX accounts require Ethiopian nationality or Ethiopian origin (yellow card).
Minimum deposit & fees: Diaspora accounts: USD 100 minimum (USD 5,000 fixed deposit); not applicable to other foreigners.
Banks accepting non-residents: none known for non-resident foreigners without Ethiopian origin; Commercial Bank of Ethiopia and others offer diaspora accounts only.
Restrictions: Strict NBE foreign-exchange controls; FX accounts limited to resident foreigners, diaspora and approved entities (FDI firms, embassies, NGOs).
Alternatives (fintech / regional): Wise/remittance services into Ethiopia; telebirr requires local ID/SIM.
Cost note: Not applicable: non-resident foreigners without Ethiopian origin cannot open accounts; diaspora accounts (USD 100 minimum, USD 5,000 fixed deposit) do not apply.

Documents required: Passport and proof of residence for in-branch opening in Asmara; no published non-resident procedure.
Minimum deposit & fees: not published
Banks accepting non-residents: none known for non-residents; Commercial Bank of Eritrea (state-owned) is the only full retail bank.
Restrictions: Strict currency controls, nakfa withdrawal limits, foreign currency must be exchanged at official rate; isolated banking system with minimal correspondent links.
Alternatives (fintech / regional): none; Wise and remittance services have very limited coverage.
Cost note: Non-residents cannot open personal accounts in Eritrea, so no cost applies and the Commercial Bank of Eritrea publishes no tariff.

Documents required: Passport, residence permit or long-stay visa, local address proof, proof of income, two photos; enhanced source-of-funds above about DJF 1 million.
Minimum deposit & fees: Minimum opening deposit required; amounts not published.
Banks accepting non-residents: BCIMR (BRED group), International Investment Bank (IIB, reported remote opening for non-residents with strict KYC).
Restrictions: DJF pegged to USD with free convertibility; AML/CFT rules require in-person verification at most banks; high barriers for non-residents.
Alternatives (fintech / regional): D-Money and Waafi mobile wallets require local SIM/ID; Wise transfers limited.
Cost note: BCIMR and IIB require a minimum opening deposit for non-residents but publish no amount, opening fee or monthly fee, so all three are null as unpublished.

Documents required: Passport or national ID, proof of address; Central Bank of Somalia requires national ID for new accounts in Banadir region.
Minimum deposit & fees: not published
Banks accepting non-residents: none known for non-Somali foreigners; Dahabshil Bank, Premier Bank, Salaam Somali Bank, IBS target Somalis and diaspora.
Restrictions: High-risk jurisdiction with limited correspondent banking; Al-Shabaab-related sanctions/AML scrutiny; economy largely USD and mobile money.
Alternatives (fintech / regional): Mobile money (EVC Plus, Zaad) and hawala remittance (Dahabshiil) via local SIM/contacts.
Cost note: Non-residents cannot open personal accounts here (banks serve Somalis and the diaspora, not other foreigners), so no costs apply.

Documents required: Passport or other ID approved by the Central Bank of Somaliland, physical address, source of funds and purpose of account declaration.
Minimum deposit & fees: Not published.
Banks accepting non-residents: Dahabshil Bank International, Premier Bank, IBS Bank (products mainly target residents and Somali diaspora).
Restrictions: Unrecognised territory with limited correspondent banking and heavy de-risking; economy runs largely on USD mobile money; no published non-resident foreigner process.
Alternatives (fintech / regional): Zaad mobile money (Telesom) and eDahab with local SIM; Dahabshiil money transfer.
Cost note: Dahabshil Bank International, Premier Bank and IBS Bank publish no non-resident fees or minimum deposit (accounts mainly in USD).

Documents required: Passport, residence or work permit, local address, in-person KYC.
Minimum deposit & fees: not published
Banks accepting non-residents: none known for non-residents (KCB, Equity Bank operate in Juba for residents and organisations).
Restrictions: Conflict-affected, severe currency instability and USD shortages; de-risking by correspondents.
Alternatives (fintech / regional): Mobile money (m-Gurush, MTN MoMo) with local SIM; hawala.
Cost note: Non-residents cannot open personal accounts here, so all cost fields are null; KCB and Equity Bank serve only residents and organisations.

Documents required: Passport, proof of address, proof of income, notarised documents; banks usually want a GOP or residence permit.
Minimum deposit & fees: Not published officially; one guide cites about USD 35,000 minimum balance at Absa Seychelles for non-residents.
Banks accepting non-residents: Absa Bank Seychelles (reported to accept non-residents with notarised documents).
Restrictions: Banks require proof of economic link; strong de-risking of offshore clients; residence/work permit usually required.
Alternatives (fintech / regional): Wise, Revolut; Mauritius or Dubai banks.
Cost note: Minimum balance is the roughly USD 35,000 for non-residents at Absa Seychelles cited by one third-party guide, not an official tariff; opening and monthly fees are not published.

Documents required: Passport (certified), proof of foreign address, bank reference or statements, source-of-funds evidence, occupation details.
Minimum deposit & fees: Not published; non-resident and private-banking accounts often expect a meaningful USD/EUR/GBP balance.
Banks accepting non-residents: MCB, SBM Bank, Absa Mauritius, AfrAsia Bank (non-resident accounts; some accept courier or introducer applications).
Restrictions: Strict KYC after FATF grey-list exit, CRS reporting; foreign-currency accounts widely available, no exchange controls.
Alternatives (fintech / regional): Introduction via licensed management company; Wise, Revolut.
Cost note: An unofficial reproduction of MCB's non-resident terms cites a USD 3,000 minimum balance to open and a USD 100 annual maintenance fee (about USD 8.30/month) plus a USD 10 penalty below minimum; the opening fee is not published and figures are unconfirmed by an official tariff.

Documents required: Passport with valid Indian visa, proof of overseas address, photograph, PAN or Form 60, and in-person KYC at an authorised dealer bank branch in India.
Minimum deposit & fees: not published
Banks accepting non-residents: Authorised dealer banks may open NRO savings/current accounts for visiting foreign nationals of non-Indian origin under FEMA; few banks advertise this, and NRE/FCNR products are restricted to NRIs/OCIs.
Restrictions: FEMA Deposit Regulations 2016 allow NRO deposits from persons resident outside India; for foreign visitors the account must be funded from abroad or by sale of foreign exchange brought in, and the balance is freely reconvertible on departure only if held 6 months or less with no local credits (otherwise RBI approval needed).
Alternatives (fintech / regional): UPI One World prepaid wallets for foreign visitors; Wise or Remitly transfers to INR.
Cost note: Authorised dealer banks may open NRO accounts for visiting foreign nationals of non-Indian origin, but no bank publishes fees or minimum balances for that route, so all three are null.

Documents required: Passport, proof of non-resident status (foreign visa/residence, entry/exit stamps), proof of profession and source of funds, CRS/FATCA forms.
Minimum deposit & fees: Roshan Digital Accounts have no or low minimum balance; fees not published for foreign nationals.
Banks accepting non-residents: Roshan Digital Account banks including HBL (NRAN account lists foreign nationals as eligible) and Standard Chartered Pakistan; others mainly require Pakistani CNIC/NICOP/POC.
Restrictions: SBP rules allow non-resident foreign nationals into RDA, but many banks limit products to Pakistani-origin customers; FX controls on outward remittances; FATF scrutiny.
Alternatives (fintech / regional): Wise to PKR accounts; JazzCash/Easypaisa need a Pakistani CNIC.
Cost note: Not published: Roshan Digital Accounts (e.g. HBL) are described as having no or low minimum balance, but opening and monthly fees for foreign nationals are not published.

Documents required: Passport, visa, proof of purpose of stay or employment, photographs, KYC form; NFCD accounts for foreign nationals per Bangladesh Bank FE rules.
Minimum deposit & fees: A secondary guide cites USD 25,000 minimum for foreign-national NFCD accounts; ordinary account fees not published.
Banks accepting non-residents: Standard Chartered Bangladesh, HSBC Bangladesh, Eastern Bank and other authorized dealer banks; non-resident foreigner acceptance not confirmed.
Restrictions: Foreign exchange regulations restrict taka accounts for non-residents to approved purposes; FX reserve pressure and repatriation controls.
Alternatives (fintech / regional): bKash or Nagad mobile money require a local SIM and national ID or passport; Wise for inbound transfers.
Cost note: A secondary guide cites a USD 25,000 minimum for foreign-national NFCD accounts (already USD); opening and monthly fees for non-resident foreigners are not published.

Documents required: Passport, proof of foreign address, source of funds; PFCA eligibility covers non-nationals visiting or intending to visit Sri Lanka, while Inward Investment Accounts (IIA, ex-SFIDA) cover non-nationals resident abroad.
Minimum deposit & fees: Not published; varies by bank and currency.
Banks accepting non-residents: DFCC Bank, Nations Trust Bank, National Savings Bank, Commercial Bank, Sampath Bank, People's Bank.
Restrictions: Foreign Exchange Act and CBSL Direction No 04 of 2021 govern permitted credits/debits; IIA funds tied to investment purposes; post-2022 crisis capital-flow controls easing.
Alternatives (fintech / regional): Wise transfers to LKR; local wallets need Sri Lankan NIC.
Cost note: No bank named publishes a non-resident personal tariff (DFCC, Nations Trust, NSB, Commercial, Sampath and People's Bank charges vary by bank and currency), so all three figures are left null as unpublished.

Documents required: Passport with valid Nepal visa, photos, application form, proof of address; account validity tied to visa period.
Minimum deposit & fees: not published
Banks accepting non-residents: Commercial banks licensed by Nepal Rastra Bank case-by-case; Machhapuchchhre Bank offers NRN foreign-currency accounts for those of Nepali origin.
Restrictions: NRB rules: tourist accounts valid only until visa expiry; NPR not freely convertible; foreign-currency withdrawal limits.
Alternatives (fintech / regional): Wise and remittance services; eSewa/Khalti wallets need local ID.
Cost note: Commercial banks open case-by-case and publish no non-resident opening fee, minimum deposit or monthly fee, and NRN accounts are for people of Nepali origin (web search budget exhausted in pass 2, so figures come from the existing min_deposit_fees text and were not re-verified against a bank tariff).

Documents required: Foreign nationals must reside in Bhutan long-term (with work permit) for a foreign currency account; remote Remit Bhutan route is for non-resident Bhutanese only.
Minimum deposit & fees: Not published.
Banks accepting non-residents: None known; Bank of Bhutan and Bhutan National Bank serve residents and Bhutanese nationals.
Restrictions: Royal Monetary Authority circular (2012) barred banks from opening deposit accounts for non-resident foreigners; tourist payments go through licensed tour operators.
Alternatives (fintech / regional): None; pay via tour operator or international cards.
Cost note: Non-residents cannot open personal accounts here, so no opening fee, deposit or monthly fee applies.

Documents required: Passport, Afghan visa and local presence; Tazkira for locals.
Minimum deposit & fees: not published
Banks accepting non-residents: none known for non-residents.
Restrictions: Taliban-run central bank under sanctions pressure; weekly withdrawal caps; most foreign correspondents refuse transfers.
Alternatives (fintech / regional): Western Union, MoneyGram (up to USD 5,000 per transaction), hawala.
Cost note: Non-residents cannot open personal accounts here, so all cost fields are null.

Documents required: Passport and supporting KYC documents submitted digitally; no work permit needed for MIB non-resident accounts.
Minimum deposit & fees: MIB non-resident foreigner account: USD 100 annual fee.
Banks accepting non-residents: Maldives Islamic Bank (Non-Resident Foreigners Deposit Account, USD only).
Restrictions: Non-resident accounts USD-only; most banks including Bank of Maldives require a valid visa or work permit.
Alternatives (fintech / regional): Wise, Revolut (no MVR local details).
Cost note: MIB Non-Resident Foreigners Deposit Account charges USD 100 a year (shown as USD 8.33/month); opening fee and current minimum deposit are not published (the USD 100-250 minimums dated from MIB's 2011 launch).

Documents required: Passport, residence permit (CERPAC), proof of Nigerian address, BVN enrolment, reference letters, passport photos.
Minimum deposit & fees: Low minimums for savings and domiciliary accounts; non-resident fees not published.
Banks accepting non-residents: Access Bank, GTBank, Zenith Bank open accounts for resident expatriates; 2025 non-resident BVN platform is for diaspora Nigerians only.
Restrictions: Mandatory BVN, CBN FX restrictions and naira volatility, domiciliary account withdrawal limits.
Alternatives (fintech / regional): Brokers' foreign-investor accounts; Wise for NGN payments; fintechs (Opay, Moniepoint) need BVN/NIN.
Cost note: Foreign non-residents cannot open personal accounts (the 2025 non-resident BVN platform is for diaspora Nigerians only), so no applicable costs.

Documents required: Passport plus Non-Citizen Ghana Card (issued only to foreigners resident at least 90 days, needing a residence permit and in-person biometrics), proof of Ghana address, and work/employment documents where applicable.
Minimum deposit & fees: Reported 2026 tariffs: Societe Generale Ghana GHS 50 current account, OmniBSIC USD 50 FX current account, Stanbic GHS 500 opening and USD 5/month on FX accounts.
Banks accepting non-residents: none known for short-stay non-residents; Absa, Stanbic, GCB, Ecobank and Standard Chartered serve foreigners once they hold a Non-Citizen Ghana Card and residence permit.
Restrictions: Bank of Ghana notice BG/GOV/SEC/2025/36 (effective 1 Dec 2025) reportedly bars financial transactions for customers without a Ghana Card or Non-Citizen Card, limiting visitors under 90 days to one-off transactions; FCA/FEA foreign-currency account rules apply.
Alternatives (fintech / regional): Wise or Remitly transfers to GHS; mobile money (MTN MoMo, Telecel Cash) requires a Ghana Card-registered SIM.
Cost note: Non-residents cannot open personal accounts without a Non-Citizen Ghana Card and residence permit, so all three are null (resident tariffs reported for 2026: Stanbic GHS 500 opening, about USD 45 at GHS 11/USD, and USD 5/month on FX accounts).

Documents required: Passport, proof of address, residence permit or carte de sejour usually requested, source-of-funds; non-resident and foreign-currency accounts need BCEAO/Treasury formalities.
Minimum deposit & fees: not published
Banks accepting non-residents: none known for non-WAEMU non-residents; diaspora accounts (BCEAO Notice 001-03-2026) cover WAEMU nationals only.
Restrictions: BCEAO exchange controls; foreign-currency accounts require Finance Ministry/BCEAO authorisation; non-resident operations subject to prior authorisation.
Alternatives (fintech / regional): Mobile money (Orange Money, MTN MoMo, Wave) requires local SIM and ID; Wise from abroad.
Cost note: Not published: no known option for non-WAEMU non-residents, and no bank publishes non-resident fees.

Documents required: Passport, embassy/consular card or carte de sejour (residence permit), proof of local address, TIN if available, initial deposit.
Minimum deposit & fees: not published
Banks accepting non-residents: Ecobank Benin, Bank of Africa (BOA) Benin, Orabank; branch visit required and non-resident acceptance case-by-case.
Restrictions: BCEAO/WAEMU foreign-exchange regulations limit non-resident accounts in XOF; strict KYC; beware remote-account scams.
Alternatives (fintech / regional): MTN MoMo or Moov Money with local SIM; Wave; Wise for XOF payouts.
Cost note: Ecobank Benin, BOA Benin and Orabank do not publish non-resident personal account opening fees, minimum deposits or monthly fees, so all figures are null.

Documents required: Passport or residence card, local address proof, Togolese phone number, sometimes TIN and proof of income, two photos; certified copies by post for diaspora accounts.
Minimum deposit & fees: Initial deposit required, amount varies by bank and is not published.
Banks accepting non-residents: Ecobank Togo (Diaspora account, online with couriered originals), Coris Bank International Togo (diaspora account), Orabank Togo (branch).
Restrictions: UEMOA/BCEAO exchange regulation (Regulation 06/2024) governs non-resident accounts with heightened documentation since 2025; diaspora products aimed mainly at Togolese abroad.
Alternatives (fintech / regional): Mobile money (Flooz/Moov, T-Money) requires local SIM; Wise transfers to XOF.
Cost note: Ecobank Togo and Coris Bank diaspora accounts require an initial deposit whose amount varies by bank and is not published, and no opening or monthly fee is published, so all three are null.

Documents required: Passport, proof of address, and justification of purpose under BCEAO non-resident account rules; details not published by banks.
Minimum deposit & fees: not published
Banks accepting non-residents: none known specifically; Coris Bank International and Ecobank Burkina operate but publish no non-resident terms.
Restrictions: BCEAO Instruction 09/07/2025/RFE governs non-resident foreign accounts and FX accounts; military government and security situation; heightened AML scrutiny.
Alternatives (fintech / regional): Mobile money (Orange Money, Moov Money) with local SIM; Wise/remittance services.
